questions.subtopic: 2A1 Establishment, funding and SEC oversight. Legal status of the Board
questions.question: A new compliance analyst at a listed retailer asks what kind of body the PCAOB is. Under Section 101, what is the Board's legal status?

options.A: A federal agency whose members and staff are U.S. government employees
options.B: A nonprofit corporation that sits outside the U.S. government
options.C: A self-regulatory body owned and funded by the registered audit firms
options.D: A division of the SEC run by its Chief Accountant

questions.key_concept: The PCAOB is a nonprofit corporation outside the federal government, overseen by the SEC and funded mainly by issuers.
questions.pre_read: Ask what kind of legal body the Act created, and who sits above it.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 101 creates the PCAOB as a nonprofit corporation and says it is not an agency or establishment of the U.S. government; its members and staff are not federal employees. The SEC oversees it from outside under Section 107. Option C is close because the Board is overseen much like a self-regulatory body, but audit firms do not own it; accounting support fees from issuers (and, since 2010, brokers and dealers) fund it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the Board has public powers. But Section 101(b) says it is not a government agency, and its members and staff are not federal officers or employees.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the SEC oversees the Board much as it oversees self-regulatory bodies, but no audit firm owns it; accounting support fees, mainly from issuers, fund it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the SEC approves Board rules and reviews its sanctions. But that is oversight from outside; the Board is a separate nonprofit corporation, not an SEC office.

tips: Eliminate: A and D both place the Board inside the federal government, but Section 101(b) says it is not a government agency or establishment.
Final two: B beats C because the Board is a nonprofit corporation funded mainly by issuers' accounting support fees, not a body owned or funded by audit firms.
Exam cue: on CSOE items, the PCAOB is a nonprofit corporation that oversees audit firms, and the SEC oversees the PCAOB.

questions.subtopic: 2A1 Establishment, funding and SEC oversight. Board composition
questions.question: Two current PCAOB members are former CPAs, and the SEC's leading candidate for a vacancy also once held a CPA license. Which course BEST complies with Section 101(e)?

options.A: Appoint the candidate once the Treasury Secretary gives consent
options.B: Appoint the candidate after the CPA license is no longer held
options.C: Appoint the candidate part-time so they can keep a small practice
options.D: Pass over this candidate for someone who has never been a CPA

questions.key_concept: Only two of the five PCAOB members may be or have been CPAs, and every member serves full time.
questions.pre_read: Count the seats already held by people with a CPA background, and read the exact wording of the limit.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 101(e)(2) allows two, and only two, members who are or have been CPAs. With two former CPAs already seated, a third person who once held a license would break the limit, so the SEC must choose someone who has never been a CPA. Option B fails because the limit counts past licensing, so surrendering the license changes nothing.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the SEC consults the Treasury Secretary on appointments. But consultation is not consent, and no one can waive the two-CPA limit.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: giving up a license seems to remove the conflict, but Section 101(e)(2) counts members who are or have been CPAs, so the candidate still counts.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting as a compromise. But members serve full time and may not engage in any other professional or business activity (Section 101(e)(3)).

tips: Eliminate: A treats Treasury consultation as a veto, and C conflicts with the full-time, no-other-business rule in Section 101(e)(3).
Final two: D beats B because the limit counts members who are or have been CPAs, so surrendering a license does not reset the count.
Exam cue: two, and only two, CPAs sit on the five-member PCAOB; read 'are or have been' literally.

questions.subtopic: 2A1 Establishment, funding and SEC oversight. Who bears the Board's costs
questions.question: During a cost review, an issuer's CFO proposes asking its audit firm to absorb the PCAOB accounting support fee. Under Section 109, who bears that fee?

options.A: Each issuer, in proportion to its average equity market capitalization
options.B: Each audit firm, in proportion to its issuer audit fees
options.C: Taxpayers, through an annual appropriation that Congress approves
options.D: Each issuer equally, as a flat charge the SEC sets

questions.key_concept: Each issuer's share of the PCAOB accounting support fee is set by its equity market capitalization.
questions.pre_read: Separate the fees audit firms pay the Board from the fee that funds the Board's budget.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 109 recovers the Board's SEC-approved budget through an annual accounting support fee allocated among issuers. Each issuer's share is its average monthly equity market capitalization over the prior 12 months, divided by the total for all issuers. Option B is close because audit firms do pay the Board, but only registration and annual fees that cover processing costs, so the issuer bears its own share.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: registered firms pay the Board registration and annual fees, but those only recover processing costs; the accounting support fee is allocated to issuers.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the Board serves a public purpose. But Section 109 says the fees are not public money and the Board is not funded by appropriations.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a flat fee sounds simple. But Section 109(g) allocates the fee by each issuer's share of total equity market capitalization.

tips: Eliminate: C contradicts Section 109's statement that the fees are not public money, and D conflicts with the market capitalization formula in Section 109(g).
Final two: A beats B because audit firms pay only cost-recovery registration and annual fees; the accounting support fee falls on issuers by market capitalization.
Exam cue: issuers' shares of the PCAOB support fee follow equity market capitalization. Taxpayers and audit firms pay none of it.

questions.subtopic: 2A1 Establishment, funding and SEC oversight. Review of a Board sanction
questions.question: The PCAOB suspends an audit firm's registration, and the firm promptly applies to the SEC for review. Which outcome BEST reflects the Act while that review is pending?

options.A: The suspension stands until a federal court rules
options.B: The suspension is final, since the SEC cannot review Board sanctions
options.C: The suspension is stayed unless the SEC orders that it apply
options.D: The suspension applies now, though the SEC may later reduce it

questions.key_concept: The SEC reviews PCAOB sanctions, and an application for review stays the sanction unless the SEC orders otherwise.
questions.pre_read: Note who reviews a Board sanction first, and what happens to the sanction while that review is pending.
questions.correct_explanation: Under Section 105(e), applying to the SEC for review of a Board disciplinary action operates as a stay of that action, unless and until the SEC orders that the stay end. The SEC then reviews the sanction and may enhance, modify, cancel or reduce it under Section 107(c). Option D is close because the SEC can reduce the sanction, but the sanction does not apply during review unless the SEC lifts the stay.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because sanctions can reach the courts eventually. But the SEC reviews Board sanctions first, and the application to the SEC itself stays the suspension.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting if the Board is seen as the final word. But Section 107(c) lets the SEC review, enhance, modify, cancel or reduce Board sanctions.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the SEC may reduce the sanction, but under Section 105(e) the application for review stays it, so it does not apply now unless the SEC orders otherwise.

tips: Eliminate: B overlooks the SEC's Section 107(c) review of Board sanctions, and A skips the SEC, which reviews Board sanctions before any court.
Final two: C beats D because an application for SEC review stays the Board's sanction under Section 105(e); the SEC must order otherwise for it to apply.
Exam cue: a Board sanction goes to the SEC for review, and asking for review pauses it unless the SEC lifts the stay.

questions.subtopic: 2A2 Registration and foreign audit firms. Starting an issuer audit
questions.question: A regional CPA firm that audits only private companies is asked to audit a newly listed issuer. Under Section 102, what must happen FIRST?

options.A: The firm completes an AICPA peer review before accepting
options.B: The firm starts the audit and registers within a year
options.C: The issuer's audit committee waives registration for this audit
options.D: The firm registers with the PCAOB before working on the audit

questions.key_concept: Only PCAOB-registered firms may prepare, issue or participate in an issuer's audit report.
questions.pre_read: Look at the firm's current client base and what it still lacks before it can work on an issuer audit.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 102(a) makes it unlawful for any firm that is not registered with the PCAOB to prepare or issue, or even participate in preparing, an audit report for an issuer. So the firm must register first; the Board acts on a completed application within 45 days. Option B is close because registration can be quick, but starting the audit before registering means participating while unregistered.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because peer review was the profession's own quality check. But for issuer audits the Act requires PCAOB registration, and the Board inspects registered firms itself.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the firm may plan to register soon, but Section 102(a) bars an unregistered firm from even participating in preparing an issuer's audit report.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the audit committee oversees the auditor. But no one can waive Section 102; the committee must hire a registered firm.

tips: Eliminate: A swaps PCAOB registration for profession-run peer review, and C gives the audit committee a waiver power the Act does not grant.
Final two: D beats B because Section 102(a) bars an unregistered firm from participating in an issuer's audit report at all, not just from signing it.
Exam cue: no PCAOB registration means no part in an issuer's audit report.

questions.subtopic: 2A2 Registration and foreign audit firms. Relying on a foreign firm
questions.question: A registered U.S. firm relied on a Brazilian firm's audit of an issuer's subsidiary, and the PCAOB now requests those workpapers. Which duty BEST describes the U.S. firm's position?

options.A: It must produce them, having secured the foreign firm's agreement
options.B: It may refer the PCAOB to the Brazilian firm to respond
options.C: It need not respond, since foreign audit work is outside PCAOB reach
options.D: It may release the papers only if the audit committee approves

questions.key_concept: A registered firm that relies on a foreign firm's audit work must produce that firm's workpapers on request.
questions.pre_read: Identify which firm relied on whose work, then ask whose duty the request triggers.
questions.correct_explanation: Under 15 U.S.C. 7216(b)(2), as amended by Dodd-Frank, a registered firm that relies on a foreign firm's work must produce that firm's workpapers when the SEC or the Board asks, and must secure the foreign firm's agreement to production as a condition of relying on it. Option B is close because the foreign firm must also produce, but that does not remove the U.S. firm's own duty.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the Brazilian firm must also produce its papers under 7216(b)(1), but the relying U.S. firm has its own duty to produce them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because home-country regulators supervise the Brazilian firm. But Section 106 subjects foreign firms involved in issuer audits to the Act and Board rules.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the audit committee oversees the auditor. But the production duty runs to the SEC and the Board, and no committee approval is needed.

tips: Eliminate: C conflicts with Section 106, which brings foreign firms in issuer audits under the Act, and D adds an audit committee approval the Act does not require.
Final two: A beats B because the relying U.S. firm must itself produce the foreign workpapers; the foreign firm's own duty does not replace it.
Exam cue: rely on a foreign firm's work, and you must be able to hand its workpapers to the SEC or the PCAOB.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Standards, inspections and discipline. Inspection schedule
questions.question: A registered audit firm regularly issues audit reports for 85 issuers. Which inspection schedule does Section 104 set for it?

options.A: Every year, since it audits more than 50 issuers
options.B: Only when the SEC requests a special inspection
options.C: At least every three years, given its client count
options.D: Once every five years, in step with partner rotation

questions.key_concept: PCAOB inspection frequency depends on how many issuers a firm audits: above 100 yearly, otherwise at least every three years.
questions.pre_read: Find the client count in the stem and compare it with the threshold in Section 104.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 104(b)(1) sets two schedules: firms that regularly provide audit reports for more than 100 issuers are inspected every year, and firms with 100 or fewer are inspected not less than once every three years. At 85 issuers, this firm falls in the second group. Option A is close because large firms are inspected yearly, but the threshold is more than 100 issuers, not 50.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: yearly inspection is real, but Section 104(b)(1)(A) applies it to firms with more than 100 issuer clients; at 85, the three-year schedule applies.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the SEC can request special inspections. But those add to the regular program; they do not replace it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because partner rotation uses five-year periods. But inspection frequency depends on the number of issuer clients, not on rotation.

tips: Eliminate: B treats special inspections as the only inspections, and D borrows the five-year partner rotation period, which does not set inspection frequency.
Final two: C beats A because yearly inspections apply only above 100 issuer clients; a firm with 85 is inspected at least every three years.
Exam cue: more than 100 issuer clients means yearly inspection; 100 or fewer means at least every three years.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Standards, inspections and discipline. Work paper retention
questions.question: The records manager at a registered audit firm is setting how long to keep issuer audit workpapers. What retention period do Section 103 and Rule 2-06 require?

options.A: Five years from the end of the fiscal period audited
options.B: Seven years after the firm concludes the audit
options.C: Until the issuer files its next annual report on Form 10-K
options.D: Three years, matching the PCAOB inspection cycle

questions.key_concept: Registered firms keep issuer audit workpapers for seven years under Section 103 and Rule 2-06.
questions.pre_read: Two retention periods appear in SOX; check which one the PCAOB standards and the SEC rule set.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 103(a)(2)(A)(i) requires PCAOB auditing standards to make firms prepare and keep audit workpapers for at least seven years, and Rule 2-06 requires records to be kept for seven years after the auditor concludes the audit. Option A is close because Section 802 (18 U.S.C. 1520(a)(1)) sets five years, but Rule 2-06, which the SEC issued under that same section, requires seven.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: 18 U.S.C. 1520(a)(1) sets five years, but Rule 2-06, issued under 1520(a)(2), requires seven, and a knowing and willful breach of it is a crime (1520(b)).
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because each annual report starts a new cycle. But the Act and SEC rules set fixed multi-year periods, not one tied to the next filing.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because smaller firms are inspected at least every three years. But inspection frequency does not set record retention; the rules require seven years.

tips: Eliminate: C ties retention to the next filing rather than a fixed period, and D borrows the three-year inspection cycle, which does not govern retention.
Final two: B beats A because Section 103 and Rule 2-06, made under Section 802 itself, require seven years; the statute's own five years is the shorter floor.
Exam cue: issuer audit workpapers are kept seven years; five years is the Section 802 trap.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Standards, inspections and discipline. Approving the audit report
questions.question: To save time, the engagement partner at a small registered firm plans to approve and release an issuer's audit report alone. Which Section 103 requirement does this plan breach?

options.A: Review of the audit report by the issuer's audit committee first
options.B: Rotation of the lead partner after five consecutive years
options.C: Clearance of each audit report by the PCAOB before release
options.D: Review and approval of the report by a second qualified partner

questions.key_concept: Section 103 requires a concurring or second-partner review and approval of each issuer audit report.
questions.pre_read: Ask who, besides the partner in charge, must sign off before an issuer audit report goes out.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 103(a)(2)(A)(ii) requires PCAOB auditing standards to include a concurring or second-partner review and approval of each audit report, and concurring approval of its issuance, by a qualified person other than the person in charge, or by an independent reviewer. A partner approving alone skips that step. Option A is close because the audit committee hears from the auditor, but it does not approve the report.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the audit committee oversees the auditor and receives Section 204 reports, but approving the audit report is the firm's second-partner review, not the committee's job.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it is another partner rule. But rotation, under Section 203, limits tenure; it says nothing about who approves a report.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the PCAOB oversees audits. But the Board inspects after the fact; it does not clear reports before release.

tips: Eliminate: B is the Section 203 tenure rule, not an approval step, and C has the PCAOB clearing reports before release, though it inspects afterwards.
Final two: D beats A because Section 103 requires a second qualified person to review and approve the report; the audit committee oversees but does not approve it.
Exam cue: under Section 103, every issuer audit report needs a second qualified reviewer's approval before release.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Standards, inspections and discipline. Sanctions and level of fault
questions.question: A PCAOB hearing finds that an audit partner was negligent once, on a single audit, with no intent, knowledge or recklessness. Which sanction does Section 105 bar the Board from imposing?

options.A: A censure of the partner for the violation
options.B: Required additional professional education or training
options.C: A permanent bar from association with any registered firm
options.D: A civil money penalty for the negligent violation

questions.key_concept: The PCAOB's heaviest sanctions require intentional, knowing or reckless conduct, or repeated negligence.
questions.pre_read: Note the level of fault the hearing found, and check which sanctions need more than that.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 105(c)(5) limits the heaviest sanctions, including suspension or revocation of registration, bars, activity limits and the higher money penalties, to intentional or knowing conduct, including recklessness, or repeated negligence. A single negligent act still allows censure, training or a money penalty within the lower tier of Section 105(c)(4)(D)(i). Option D is close because money penalties sound severe, but only the higher tier needs that level of fault.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because censure sounds serious. But censure is among the lesser sanctions in Section 105(c)(4), available for a single negligent violation.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as a remedial step. But required education or training is a lesser sanction the Board may impose without intent or repeated negligence.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: Section 105(c)(5) restricts only the higher penalty tier; a money penalty within the lower tier remains available for one negligent act.

tips: Eliminate: A and B are lesser sanctions in Section 105(c)(4) that need no intent, knowledge or repeated negligence.
Final two: C beats D because a bar needs intentional, knowing or reckless conduct, or repeated negligence; a lower-tier money penalty does not.
Exam cue: one negligent act allows the lighter sanctions; revocation, bars and top penalties need intent, recklessness or repeated negligence.

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Accounting standards and PCAOB rulemaking. Source of accounting principles
questions.question: An issuer's new audit committee member assumes the PCAOB writes the accounting principles used in the company's financial statements. Which statement BEST corrects this under Section 108?

options.A: The SEC recognizes FASB's standards as generally accepted principles
options.B: The PCAOB sets accounting principles alongside its auditing standards
options.C: Each issuer's auditor chooses the principles that apply to the audit
options.D: The SEC writes all accounting principles itself, by formal rule

questions.key_concept: Under Section 108 the SEC recognizes FASB's accounting standards; the PCAOB sets auditing standards.
questions.pre_read: Separate the rules for preparing financial statements from the rules for auditing them.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 108 lets the SEC recognize, as generally accepted for the securities laws, the accounting principles of a private standard setter that meets set criteria. In its 2003 policy statement, Release No. 33-8221, the SEC recognized FASB's standards. The PCAOB sets auditing standards. Option D is close because the SEC keeps its own power over accounting principles, but it relies on FASB's standards.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the PCAOB sets standards. But its standards are auditing, quality control, ethics and independence standards for audit firms, not accounting principles.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because auditors judge whether principles were applied. But management prepares the statements under recognized principles; the auditor does not choose them.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: Section 108(c) keeps the SEC's own authority, but under Section 108 the SEC recognizes FASB's standards rather than writing all principles itself.

tips: Eliminate: B confuses the PCAOB's auditing standards with accounting principles, and C gives the auditor a choice that belongs to the recognized standards management applies.
Final two: A beats D because the SEC keeps authority over accounting principles but, under Section 108, recognizes FASB's standards as generally accepted.
Exam cue: FASB writes the accounting rules, the PCAOB writes the auditing rules, and the SEC stands over both.

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Accounting standards and PCAOB rulemaking. When a Board standard binds
questions.question: The PCAOB has just adopted a new auditing standard, and a registered firm's methodology team asks about timing. Under Section 107, when will it bind the firm's issuer audits?

options.A: On the effective date the Board sets when it adopts the standard
options.B: Only after the SEC approves it and its effective date arrives
options.C: Once Congress reviews it under the Congressional Review Act
options.D: When each issuer's audit committee votes to accept the standard

questions.key_concept: No PCAOB rule or standard takes effect until the SEC approves it.
questions.pre_read: Ask which body must act after the Board adopts a standard before it binds anyone.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 107(b)(2) says no PCAOB rule, including an auditing standard, takes effect without the SEC's prior approval. The SEC publishes notice, takes public comment and approves the rule if it meets the Act's criteria. Option A is close because the Board does adopt the standard, but adoption alone binds no one until the SEC approves it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: adoption by the Board is a real step, but under Section 107(b)(2) no Board rule takes effect without prior SEC approval.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because some federal rules go to Congress. But the Act sends PCAOB rules to the SEC for approval.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the audit committee oversees the auditor. But PCAOB standards bind registered firms once SEC-approved and effective; audit committees do not vote on them.

tips: Eliminate: C sends Board rules to Congress instead of the SEC, and D gives audit committees a veto over auditing standards that the Act does not give them.
Final two: B beats A because Section 107(b)(2) makes SEC approval a condition of any Board rule taking effect; Board adoption alone is not enough.
Exam cue: the PCAOB adopts, the SEC approves, and only then does the rule take effect.

questions.subtopic: 2B1 Prohibited services and preapproval. Internal audit work by the auditor
questions.question: An issuer's CFO wants its audit firm to take over the outsourced internal audit of financial reporting controls this year. Which statement BEST reflects Section 201?

options.A: The firm may not provide it while it audits the issuer
options.B: The firm may provide it if the audit committee preapproves it
options.C: The firm may provide it if fees stay under 5%
options.D: The firm may not provide it without the CFO's written approval

questions.key_concept: An issuer's auditor may not provide internal audit outsourcing during the audit, even with audit committee approval.
questions.pre_read: Check whether the service is on the prohibited list before asking who approves it.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 201 adds Exchange Act Section 10A(g), which makes it unlawful for an issuer's registered auditor to provide internal audit outsourcing services at the same time as the audit. SEC Rule 2-01(c)(4)(v) applies the ban to internal audit work on internal accounting controls, financial systems or financial statements. Option B is close because preapproval governs permitted services, but it cannot make a prohibited service allowable.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: audit committee preapproval is required for permitted non-audit services, such as tax work, but it cannot cure a service on the prohibited list.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because of the 5% de minimis exception. But that exception only waives preapproval for permitted services; it does not lift a prohibition.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the CFO runs finance. But management has no approval role for auditor services, and for prohibited services no approval helps.

tips: Eliminate: C applies the de minimis waiver, which only excuses missing preapproval, and D gives management an approval role the Act gives the audit committee.
Final two: A beats B because internal audit outsourcing is on the Section 201 prohibited list; preapproval only covers non-audit services that are not prohibited.
Exam cue: no approval cures a prohibited service; a permitted service needs audit committee preapproval.

questions.subtopic: 2B1 Prohibited services and preapproval. Tax work by the auditor
questions.question: A manufacturer's controller wants to hire the company's independent auditor for corporate tax compliance work. Under Title II of the Act, what is required FIRST, before the work starts?

options.A: No step can help, since tax work is a prohibited service
options.B: Written approval from the CFO, who manages the auditor relationship
options.C: Advance approval from the issuer's audit committee
options.D: A case-by-case exemption that the PCAOB grants for it

questions.key_concept: Routine tax compliance work by the issuer's auditor needs the audit committee's advance approval.
questions.pre_read: Decide first whether tax work is banned or permitted, then who must approve it.
questions.correct_explanation: Tax services are not on the Section 201 prohibited list. Section 201 names them as non-audit services the auditor may provide if the audit committee approves them in advance, and Section 202 requires that preapproval. Option D is close because the PCAOB can grant case-by-case exemptions, but those apply to prohibited services; permitted tax work needs the audit committee's approval, not the Board's.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because many non-audit services are banned. But Section 201 expressly names tax services as permitted with audit committee preapproval.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the CFO manages the relationship day to day. But preapproval belongs to the audit committee, and SEC rules bar delegating it to management.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: Section 201(b) lets the PCAOB exempt services from the prohibitions case by case, but tax work is not prohibited and needs audit committee preapproval.

tips: Eliminate: A wrongly puts tax work on the prohibited list, and B gives management a preapproval role that belongs to the audit committee.
Final two: C beats D because the PCAOB's exemption power covers prohibited services; permitted tax work needs the audit committee's advance approval.
Exam cue: tax work by the auditor is allowed, but only with audit committee preapproval.

questions.subtopic: 2B1 Prohibited services and preapproval. An overlooked small service
questions.question: Mid-audit, an issuer finds its auditor did a permitted advisory job nobody recognized as non-audit when engaged; fees were 3% of the year's auditor fees. Under Section 202, what keeps the de minimis exception available?

options.A: Report it to the PCAOB, which may grant the waiver
options.B: Get prompt audit committee approval before the audit ends
options.C: Have the CFO approve it in writing before the audit ends
options.D: Take no action, because fees under 5% need no approval

questions.key_concept: The de minimis exception needs low fees, an unrecognized service and audit committee approval before the audit is completed.
questions.pre_read: List the conditions of the exception and check which one the stem has not yet met.
questions.correct_explanation: The de minimis exception in Section 10A(i)(1)(B) needs three conditions: the services total no more than 5% of the revenues the issuer paid its auditor that year, they were not recognized as non-audit services at engagement, and they are promptly brought to the audit committee and approved, by it or a delegated member, before the audit is completed. Option D is close because the 5% test is met, but it is only one condition.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the PCAOB can exempt prohibited services. But the de minimis waiver is set by statute and turns on audit committee approval, not the Board.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the CFO oversees finance. But only the audit committee, or a member it delegates to, can approve the service under Section 202.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the 3% fee meets the 5% test, but the exception also needs prompt audit committee approval before the audit is completed.

tips: Eliminate: A sends the matter to the PCAOB, which has no role in this waiver, and C relies on management approval, which Section 202 does not allow.
Final two: B beats D because the 5% test is only one of three conditions; the audit committee must still approve before the audit is completed.
Exam cue: de minimis needs all three: 5% or less, unrecognized at engagement, and committee approval before the audit ends.

questions.subtopic: 2B1 Prohibited services and preapproval. Delegating approval of auditor services
questions.question: An audit committee's policy lets the CFO approve any non-audit engagement with the auditor under $50,000 and report to the committee quarterly. Which change BEST brings the policy within Section 202 and SEC rules?

options.A: Lower the limit to $10,000 so each approval counts as de minimis
options.B: Have the full board ratify the CFO's approvals each year
options.C: Have the CFO's approvals reported at every committee meeting
options.D: Delegate approval to an independent director on the committee

questions.key_concept: Audit committees may delegate preapproval to their independent members, never to management.
questions.pre_read: Find who actually approves the engagements under the policy, and who the Act allows to approve them.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 202 lets the audit committee delegate preapproval only to one or more of its members who are independent directors, whose decisions go to the full committee at each scheduled meeting. SEC Rule 2-01(c)(7) also bars preapproval policies that delegate the committee's duties to management. Option C is close because it adds timely reporting, but the CFO, a member of management, would still be approving.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the de minimis exception involves small amounts. But it is a 5% test on unrecognized services, not a dollar limit a committee can set.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the board outranks the committee. But yearly ratification comes after the work; preapproval must come before the engagement.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: reporting at each meeting matches the rule for delegated approvals, but the delegate must be an independent director on the committee, not the CFO.

tips: Eliminate: A misreads the de minimis exception as a dollar limit, and B approves engagements after the fact, which is not preapproval.
Final two: D beats C because only independent directors on the audit committee may receive delegated preapproval; reporting cannot fix approval by management.
Exam cue: preapproval can be delegated within the audit committee, never to management.

questions.subtopic: 2B2 Partner rotation and auditor reports to the audit committee. Who must rotate
questions.question: At an issuer, the audit partner responsible for reviewing the audit has served in each of the last five fiscal years; the lead partner already rotated. What does Section 203 require for the next audit?

options.A: A different partner must take over the reviewing role
options.B: The audit firm itself must be replaced for the next audit
options.C: Only lead partners rotate, so the reviewer may continue
options.D: The reviewer may continue if the audit committee agrees

questions.key_concept: Both the lead partner and the reviewing partner must rotate after five consecutive years on an issuer audit.
questions.pre_read: Count the reviewer's years, then check which partner roles the rotation rule names.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 203 makes it unlawful for a registered firm to audit an issuer if the lead partner or the partner responsible for reviewing the audit has performed audit services for that issuer in each of the five previous fiscal years. SEC Rule 2-01(c)(6) applies the same five-year limit to the engagement quality reviewer, followed by a five-year time-out. Option C is close but leaves out the reviewing partner.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because rotation is often discussed for firms. But the Act rotates partners; firm rotation was only studied under Section 207.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the lead partner must rotate, but Section 203 also names the partner responsible for reviewing the audit, so the reviewer rotates too.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the audit committee oversees the auditor. But Section 203 has no audit committee waiver; continuing would make the audit unlawful.

tips: Eliminate: B turns partner rotation into firm rotation, which the Act only studied, and D adds an audit committee waiver that Section 203 does not contain.
Final two: A beats C because Section 203 covers both the lead partner and the reviewing partner after five consecutive years.
Exam cue: two partners rotate after five years, the lead and the reviewer; the firm does not.

questions.subtopic: 2B2 Partner rotation and auditor reports to the audit committee. Reporting accounting alternatives
questions.question: Before an issuer files its annual report, its auditor and management discussed two acceptable GAAP treatments for a lease portfolio. Under Section 204, what must the auditor report to the audit committee MOST specifically?

options.A: Only management's chosen treatment and its effect
options.B: Nothing, because both treatments are acceptable under GAAP
options.C: Each alternative, its effects and the firm's preference
options.D: A summary sent to the CFO for forwarding to the committee

questions.key_concept: Auditors must report alternative GAAP treatments, their ramifications and the firm's preference directly to the audit committee.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the audit committee needs to judge management's accounting choice for itself.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 204 requires the registered firm to report to the audit committee all alternative GAAP treatments discussed with management, the ramifications of using them, and the treatment the firm prefers, along with critical accounting policies and other material written communications. SEC Rule 2-07 requires this before the audit report is filed. Option A is close but leaves out the alternative and the firm's own preference.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: management's chosen treatment is part of the story, but Section 204 requires all alternatives discussed, their ramifications and the firm's preference.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because both treatments are acceptable. But Section 204 targets exactly that case: alternatives within GAAP discussed with management.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the CFO works with the auditor daily. But the report goes directly to the audit committee, not through management.

tips: Eliminate: B misses that Section 204 covers alternatives within GAAP, and D routes the report through the CFO instead of directly to the audit committee.
Final two: C beats A because Section 204 requires every alternative discussed, its ramifications and the firm's preferred treatment, not just management's choice.
Exam cue: the auditor tells the audit committee what it discussed with management and what it would prefer.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Conflicts of interest, studies and state regulators. Hiring from the audit team
questions.question: Priya, a senior manager at Alder LLP, worked throughout the audit of Rivera, an issuer, in the year before this audit began, and now joins Rivera as CFO. What BEST applies under Section 206?

options.A: Alder may continue if a different partner leads the audit
options.B: Alder may continue, since the rule covers only former partners
options.C: Alder may not continue unless Rivera's audit committee approves
options.D: Alder may not do the current audit, since Priya worked on it

questions.key_concept: A firm cannot audit an issuer whose top finance officer worked on its audit at the firm in the year before the audit began.
questions.pre_read: Note Priya's new role and when Priya last worked on the audit.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 206 makes it unlawful for a registered firm to audit an issuer whose CEO, controller, CFO, chief accounting officer or equivalent was employed by the firm and took part in any capacity in the issuer's audit during the one-year period before the audit began. Priya did, so Alder cannot perform this audit. Option C is close, but Section 206 has no audit committee approval route for an ordinary hire.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because rotation addresses other familiarity risks. But the bar turns on Priya's role at Rivera, not on who leads Alder's team.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because partners have the most influence. But Section 206 covers anyone employed by the firm who took part in the audit in any capacity.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the SEC rule lets an audit committee act only in emergencies or unusual situations; for an ordinary CFO hire, Section 206 bars the audit regardless of approval.

tips: Eliminate: A treats partner rotation as a cure, and B narrows the rule to partners, though it covers participation in any capacity.
Final two: D beats C because Section 206 bars the audit outright for an ordinary hire; audit committee approval does not lift the cooling-off period.
Exam cue: worked on the audit within the past year and now a top finance officer at the client? The firm cannot do that audit.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Conflicts of interest, studies and state regulators. Audit firm rotation
questions.question: A director asks how Title II dealt with making issuers change audit firms periodically. Which body did Section 207 task with studying mandatory firm rotation?

options.A: The PCAOB, through a rulemaking on audit firm tenure
options.B: The Comptroller General, through a study for Congress
options.C: The SEC, through final rules due within 180 days
options.D: Each issuer's audit committee, through an annual review

questions.key_concept: Section 207 ordered a Comptroller General study of mandatory firm rotation instead of requiring it.
questions.pre_read: Separate what Title II required from what it only asked someone to study.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 207 directed the Comptroller General, who heads the Government Accountability Office, to study the potential effects of requiring mandatory rotation of registered audit firms and to report to Congress within one year. The Act itself rotates partners, not firms. Option A is close because the PCAOB writes standards for audit firms, but Section 207 gave the study to the Comptroller General.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the PCAOB sets rules for registered firms, but Section 207 assigned the firm rotation study to the Comptroller General, not the Board.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because Section 208 required SEC rules within 180 days. But those rules carried out Section 10A(g) to (l); they were not a rotation study.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because audit committees appoint and oversee the auditor. But Section 207 called for a national study, not a company-level review.

tips: Eliminate: C mixes in Section 208's 180-day SEC rules, and D confuses a national study with an audit committee's own oversight.
Final two: B beats A because Section 207 named the Comptroller General to study firm rotation; the PCAOB was not given that study.
Exam cue: Title II rotates partners; firm rotation was only studied, by the Comptroller General.

questions.subtopic: 2A1 Establishment, funding and SEC oversight. Use of Board penalty money
questions.question: The PCAOB collects a civil money penalty from a registered audit firm after a disciplinary hearing. Under Section 109(c)(2), how must the Board use the funds it collects?

options.A: To lower the accounting support fees that issuers pay the next year
options.B: To fund merit scholarships for students in accredited accounting programs
options.C: To pay into a fair fund for investors hurt by the audit
options.D: To pay whistleblower awards through the SEC's investor protection fund

questions.key_concept: Money penalties the PCAOB collects fund merit scholarships for accounting students; they do not offset the Board's budget.
questions.pre_read: Ask who collected the penalty, the PCAOB or the SEC, and what the Act says about that body's penalty money.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 109(c)(2) directs that all money penalties the Board collects fund a merit scholarship program for undergraduate and graduate students in accredited accounting degree programs, subject to advance appropriation. The money does not flow back into the Board's budget. Option A is close because Section 109(c)(1) offsets the Board's budget with firms' registration and annual fees, but penalty money is not used that way.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: Section 109(c)(1) reduces the budget recovered from issuers by firms' registration and annual fees, not by penalties; penalty money goes to accounting scholarships.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because Section 308 fair funds help harmed investors. But that applies to civil penalties the SEC obtains, not to money the PCAOB collects.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the SEC pays whistleblower awards from its own fund under Exchange Act Section 21F. Board penalties are not paid into it.

tips: Eliminate: C borrows Section 308's fair funds, which hold SEC penalties, and D borrows the SEC's whistleblower fund; neither receives PCAOB penalty money.
Final two: B beats A because Section 109(c)(2) sends Board penalties to accounting scholarships; only registration and annual fees offset the Board's budget.
Exam cue: PCAOB penalty money funds accounting scholarships; SEC penalty money can go to fair funds for harmed investors.

questions.subtopic: 2A1 Establishment, funding and SEC oversight. Who may chair the Board
questions.question: The SEC wants to name as PCAOB chairperson a CPA who stopped practicing three years ago, filling one of the two CPA seats. Under Section 101(e), when may this person serve as chair?

options.A: Now, since they no longer practice as a certified public accountant
options.B: Never, since a CPA member may not chair the Board
options.C: Once the Senate confirms them for the chair role
options.D: Once five years have passed since they last practiced

questions.key_concept: A PCAOB chair who is or was a CPA must not have practiced as one for at least five years before appointment.
questions.pre_read: Note how long ago the candidate stopped practicing and which seat they would fill.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 101(e)(2) allows two, and only two, Board members who are or have been CPAs, and if one of them is the chair, that person must not have been a practicing CPA for at least five years before appointment. Three years out of practice is not enough, so this person can chair only once five years have passed. Option A is close, but leaving practice does not end the waiting period.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: having stopped practicing is necessary but not enough; a CPA chair must have been out of practice for at least five years before appointment.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the Act limits CPAs on the Board. But Section 101(e)(2) lets one of the two CPA members chair, after five years out of practice.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because many federal officials need Senate confirmation. But the SEC appoints Board members, after consulting the Fed chair and the Treasury Secretary.

tips: Eliminate: B misreads the two-CPA limit as a ban on a CPA chair, and C adds Senate confirmation, though the SEC appoints Board members.
Final two: D beats A because Section 101(e)(2) requires a CPA chair to have been out of practice for at least five years before appointment, not merely out of practice.
Exam cue: on PCAOB membership items, keep two numbers apart: two CPA members at most, and five years out of practice for a CPA chair.

questions.subtopic: 2A1 Establishment, funding and SEC oversight. Members' ties to audit firms
questions.question: A former audit firm partner joins the PCAOB as a full-time member. Under Section 101(e)(3), while serving, the member may receive from a public accounting firm:

options.A: fixed continuing payments under a standard retirement plan
options.B: no payments of any kind, retirement benefits included
options.C: a share of its profits, if disclosed to the SEC
options.D: fees for part-time advisory work on audits of private companies

questions.key_concept: PCAOB members serve full time and may take no audit firm payments except fixed payments under standard retirement arrangements.
questions.pre_read: Note the member's past tie to an audit firm, then ask which financial links the Act cuts.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 101(e)(3) makes Board service full time: a member may hold no other job or business activity and may not share in a public accounting firm's profits or receive payments from it, except fixed continuing payments under standard arrangements for retiring firm members, on conditions the SEC may set. Option B is close because the rule is strict, but it keeps fixed retirement payments.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the rule bars profit sharing and other firm payments, but Section 101(e)(3) expressly allows fixed continuing payments under standard retirement arrangements.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because disclosure often cures conflicts. But Section 101(e)(3) bars any share in a firm's profits; disclosure to the SEC does not permit it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the work would avoid issuer audits. But members serve full time and may engage in no other professional or business activity.

tips: Eliminate: C lets disclosure cure profit sharing, and D allows part-time work, though members serve full time with no other business activity.
Final two: A beats B because Section 101(e)(3) bars profit sharing and other firm payments but keeps fixed payments under standard retirement arrangements.
Exam cue: PCAOB members are full-time and cut financial ties with audit firms; the one exception is a fixed retirement payment.

questions.subtopic: 2A2 Registration and foreign audit firms. Repeated non-inspection years
questions.question: The SEC has determined that Corlis Trading has two consecutive non-inspection years under Section 104(i), because a foreign authority's position keeps the PCAOB from inspecting its auditor's foreign office. What must the SEC now do?

options.A: Wait for a third consecutive non-inspection year before any trading ban
options.B: Bar exchange trading but let the shares trade over the counter
options.C: Prohibit trading in its securities on exchanges and over the counter
options.D: Ask the PCAOB to suspend Corlis's registration as an issuer

questions.key_concept: After two consecutive non-inspection years, the SEC must prohibit trading in the issuer's securities, on exchanges and over the counter.
questions.pre_read: Count the identified years under the law as amended, then ask which markets the consequence reaches.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 104(i)(3), as amended in December 2022, requires the SEC to prohibit trading in a covered issuer's securities after two consecutive non-inspection years, both on national exchanges and over the counter. The ban lifts once the issuer certifies it has retained a firm the Board has inspected. Option A is close because the 2020 law said three years, but the 2022 amendment cut the trigger to two.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the original 2020 text required three years, but the December 2022 amendment cut the trigger to two consecutive non-inspection years.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because delisting is the familiar sanction. But Section 104(i)(3) bars trading on exchanges and through any other SEC-regulated method, including over the counter.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the PCAOB registers audit firms. But issuers do not register with the Board; the trading ban is the SEC's action against the issuer's securities.

tips: Eliminate: B leaves over-the-counter trading open, though the ban covers it, and D treats the issuer as a PCAOB registrant, which only audit firms are.
Final two: C beats A because the December 2022 amendment cut the trigger from three to two consecutive non-inspection years.
Exam cue: an auditor the PCAOB cannot inspect for two years running means an SEC trading ban on the issuer, exchange and over-the-counter alike.

questions.subtopic: 2A2 Registration and foreign audit firms. Duty once an issuer is identified
questions.question: The SEC identifies an issuer under Section 104(i) because the PCAOB cannot inspect the foreign office of its independent auditor. Under that Section, the issuer must:

options.A: document that no government entity there owns or controls it
options.B: replace its auditor before it files its next annual report
options.C: pay the PCAOB for a special inspection of that office
options.D: delist its shares from every U.S. exchange within 90 days

questions.key_concept: An identified issuer must document that no government entity in the auditor's foreign jurisdiction owns or controls it.
questions.pre_read: Separate what identification triggers at once from what follows after repeated identification.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 104(i)(2)(B) requires each identified issuer to submit documentation showing that a governmental entity in the foreign jurisdiction does not own or control it. Identification alone does not force an auditor change; two consecutive non-inspection years bring an SEC trading ban, which ends when the issuer certifies it has retained a firm the Board has inspected. So option B is a strategy, not the duty.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: moving to a firm the Board can inspect is how an issuer avoids or ends a trading ban, but identification itself requires only the ownership documentation.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the Board can hold special inspections. But it starts them itself or at the SEC's request; the Act gives issuers no paid inspection route.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a ban can follow. But it comes only after two consecutive non-inspection years, and the SEC imposes it; there is no 90-day delisting duty.

tips: Eliminate: C invents an issuer-paid inspection, and D invents a 90-day delisting duty; the Act's consequence is an SEC trading ban after two consecutive non-inspection years.
Final two: A beats B because Section 104(i)(2)(B) requires government-ownership documentation once identified; an auditor change is a choice until a ban looms.

questions.subtopic: 2A2 Registration and foreign audit firms. Reaching a foreign firm
questions.question: A Mexican accounting firm performs material audit work that a registered U.S. firm relies on for an issuer's audit. Under Section 106(d), added by Dodd-Frank in 2010, what must the Mexican firm designate?

options.A: Its home-country audit regulator to receive SEC or Board requests
options.B: An agent in the United States to receive SEC or Board requests
options.C: The issuer's audit committee to receive SEC or Board requests
options.D: The issuer's general counsel to receive SEC or Board requests

questions.key_concept: A foreign firm doing material audit work that a registered firm relies on must designate a U.S. agent for SEC and Board requests.
questions.pre_read: Note which firm did the work and which regulators may need to reach it.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 106(d)(2), added by Dodd-Frank in 2010, requires a foreign firm that performs material services a registered firm relies on, or that does audit work, to designate to the SEC or the Board an agent in the United States who can receive their requests and enforcement papers. Option A is close because Section 106(f) lets staff accept production through foreign counterparts, but that is an alternate means, not the required agent.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: Section 106(f) lets SEC or Board staff accept production through foreign counterparts, but the firm must still designate an agent in the United States.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the audit committee oversees the auditor. But Section 106(d) puts the duty on the foreign firm, and its agent must be in the United States.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because counsel often receives legal papers. But the issuer's lawyer does not act for the foreign audit firm; Section 106(d) requires the firm's own U.S. agent.

tips: Eliminate: C and D make the issuer's own people the foreign firm's agents, though Section 106(d) puts the duty on the foreign firm itself.
Final two: B beats A because Section 106(d)(2) requires an agent in the United States; production through foreign counterparts under Section 106(f) is an optional alternate means.
Exam cue: foreign firms that work on issuer audits answer to the SEC and the PCAOB like U.S. firms, through workpapers on request and a U.S. agent.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Standards, inspections and discipline. Public parts of an inspection report
questions.question: A PCAOB inspection report criticizes a registered firm's quality control over client acceptance. Under Section 104(g), when do those criticisms stay out of the public portion of the report?

options.A: When the firm attaches a written response disputing each of them
options.B: When the firm's issuer clients agree in writing to keep them private
options.C: When the firm fixes them to the Board's satisfaction within 12 months
options.D: When the firm convinces the SEC that publishing them harms its business

questions.key_concept: Quality control criticisms in a PCAOB inspection report stay private only if the firm fixes them to the Board's satisfaction within 12 months.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the firm must do, and by when, for criticisms of its quality control to stay out of public view.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 104(g)(2) keeps out of the public report any portion that criticizes, or points to defects in, the firm's quality control system if the firm addresses them to the Board's satisfaction no later than 12 months after the report date. Option A is close because the firm's response is attached to the report under Section 104(f), but a response alone does not keep criticisms private.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: Section 104(f) attaches the firm's response to the report, but only fixing the criticisms to the Board's satisfaction within 12 months keeps them private.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because client information is confidential. But the Act ties the privacy of quality control criticisms to the firm's remediation, not to client consent.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the SEC oversees the Board. But Section 104(g)(2) turns on the firm fixing the defects within 12 months, not on harm to the firm.

tips: Eliminate: B makes privacy depend on clients' consent and D on harm to the firm; Section 104(g)(2) turns on the firm's own remediation.
Final two: C beats A because only fixing the criticisms to the Board's satisfaction within 12 months keeps them out of the public report.
Exam cue: PCAOB quality control criticisms go public unless the firm fixes them within 12 months.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Standards, inspections and discipline. Disputing a final inspection report
questions.question: A registered firm answered the PCAOB's draft inspection findings but still disputes the assessments in the final version. Under Section 104(h), what recourse does the firm have?

options.A: It may seek SEC review of the assessments within 30 days
options.B: It may ask a federal appeals court to set the report aside
options.C: It may append its written reply, but no further review exists
options.D: It may demand a public hearing on the assessments before the Board

questions.key_concept: A firm that disputes a final PCAOB inspection report after responding to the draft may seek SEC review within 30 days.
questions.pre_read: Note what the firm has already done and which body the Act places above the Board.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 104(h) lets a firm that responded to a draft inspection report, and disagrees with the final report's assessments, seek SEC review within 30 days after that event. The SEC's decision is not then reviewable in court. Option C is close because Section 104(f) attaches the firm's redacted response to the report, but the firm can also ask the SEC to review the assessments.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because SEC orders often go to courts of appeals. But Section 104(h) sends inspection disputes to the SEC, and its decision there is not court-reviewable.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: Section 104(f) does make the firm's reply part of the report, but Section 104(h) also lets the firm seek SEC review within 30 days.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because disciplinary cases get hearings. But an inspection is not a disciplinary proceeding; the Act's route for disputing a final inspection report is SEC review.

tips: Eliminate: B sends the dispute to a court, though the SEC's review decision is not court-reviewable, and D treats an inspection like a disciplinary hearing.
Final two: A beats C because Section 104(h) adds SEC review within 30 days on top of the response attached under Section 104(f).
Exam cue: on PCAOB oversight items, the SEC sits above the Board; disputes over Board inspections and sanctions go to the SEC.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Standards, inspections and discipline. Refusing to cooperate
questions.question: A senior audit partner at a registered firm will not hand over engagement workpapers or appear when PCAOB investigators ask. Under Section 105(b)(3), what may the Board do about the partner?

options.A: Refer the partner directly to the Justice Department for prosecution
options.B: Suspend or bar the partner from association with registered firms
options.C: Ask the SEC for a subpoena, since the Board has no sanction
options.D: Fine the issuer client whose audit the partner worked on

questions.key_concept: The PCAOB may suspend or bar a registered firm's associated person who refuses to cooperate with its investigation.
questions.pre_read: Note who refused and whether that person is within the Board's direct reach.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 105(b)(3) lets the Board act when a registered firm or an associated person refuses to testify, produce documents or otherwise cooperate: it may suspend or bar the person from association with any registered firm, suspend or revoke the firm's registration, or impose lesser sanctions. Option C is close because the Board can ask the SEC for subpoenas, but it also has this sanction of its own.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because refusals can obstruct justice. But the Board refers matters to the Justice Department only at the SEC's direction (Section 105(b)(4)); its direct tool is a sanction.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the Board may seek SEC subpoenas, but Section 105(b)(3) also gives it a sanction of its own: suspending or barring a person who refuses to cooperate.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the client's audit is at issue. But the PCAOB disciplines registered firms and their associated persons, not issuers.

tips: Eliminate: A skips the SEC, which must direct any referral to the Justice Department, and D aims at the issuer, which the PCAOB does not discipline.
Final two: B beats C because Section 105(b)(3) gives the Board its own sanction for noncooperation; an SEC subpoena is an extra tool, not the only one.
Exam cue: registered firms and their people consent to cooperate when the firm registers; refusing can cost them their association or registration.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Standards, inspections and discipline. Hiring a barred person
questions.question: The PCAOB has permanently barred Morgan, a former audit partner, from association with registered firms, and a listed retailer that knows this wants Morgan as its controller. What does Section 105(c)(7) provide?

options.A: The retailer may hire Morgan; the Board regulates firms, not issuers
options.B: The retailer may hire Morgan one year after the bar took effect
options.C: The retailer may not hire Morgan unless its audit committee approves
options.D: The retailer may not hire Morgan unless the Board or SEC consents

questions.key_concept: A person barred by the PCAOB may not take an accounting or financial management role at an issuer without Board or SEC consent.
questions.pre_read: Note the role Morgan would take and whether the retailer knows of the bar.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 105(c)(7)(B), as amended in 2010, makes it unlawful for a person barred from association with registered firms to willfully become associated with an issuer in an accountancy or financial management capacity, and unlawful for an issuer that knew, or should have known, of the bar to permit it, without the consent of the Board or the SEC. Option C is close, but an audit committee cannot give that consent.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the PCAOB oversees audit firms, not issuers. But Section 105(c)(7)(B) makes it unlawful for an issuer that knows of a bar to permit this association.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because Section 206 sets a one-year cooling-off period for hires from the audit team. A permanent PCAOB bar is different and does not lapse after a year.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the hire does need consent, but Section 105(c)(7)(B) names only the Board or the SEC, not the issuer's own audit committee.

tips: Eliminate: A treats the Board's reach as ending at audit firms, though the bar binds issuers that know of it, and B borrows Section 206's one-year cooling-off period.
Final two: D beats C because Section 105(c)(7)(B) allows the association only with Board or SEC consent; the issuer's audit committee cannot lift a PCAOB bar.
Exam cue: a PCAOB bar follows the person into an issuer's finance and accounting roles; only the Board or the SEC can consent.

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Accounting standards and PCAOB rulemaking. New Board rules and emerging growth company audits
questions.question: The SEC approved a 2025 PCAOB auditing rule without determining that it should apply to emerging growth company audits. Under Section 103(a)(3)(C), does it apply to the audit of Ostrander Bio, an emerging growth company?

options.A: Yes; SEC approval makes a Board rule binding on every issuer audit
options.B: Yes, if Ostrander's audit committee elects to apply the new rule
options.C: No; Ostrander is audited under AICPA private company standards
options.D: No; post-April 2012 rules need an SEC decision for these audits

questions.key_concept: PCAOB rules adopted after April 5, 2012 apply to an emerging growth company's audit only if the SEC determines they should.
questions.pre_read: Note the issuer's status and when the rule was adopted, then ask what the SEC decided.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 103(a)(3)(C), added by JOBS Act Section 104 in 2012, says a Board rule adopted after April 5, 2012 does not apply to an emerging growth company's audit unless the SEC determines it should, weighing investor protection and efficiency, competition and capital formation. Without that determination, the rule does not reach Ostrander's audit. Option A is close because every Board rule needs SEC approval, but approval alone does not reach emerging growth company audits.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: every Board rule needs SEC approval to take effect, but for emerging growth company audits a post-April 2012 rule also needs a specific SEC determination.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the audit committee oversees the auditor. But it does not choose which PCAOB rules apply; the Act and the SEC's determination decide that.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because emerging growth companies get scaled rules. But an emerging growth company is still an issuer, so a registered firm audits it under the PCAOB standards that apply.

tips: Eliminate: B lets the audit committee pick auditing rules, and C moves an issuer's audit to private company standards; an emerging growth company is still audited under PCAOB standards.
Final two: D beats A because Section 103(a)(3)(C) requires a separate SEC determination before a post-April 2012 Board rule reaches emerging growth company audits.
Exam cue: an emerging growth company in the stem? Check whether the rule is newer than April 5, 2012 and whether the SEC extended it to emerging growth company audits.

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Accounting standards and PCAOB rulemaking. Named rule types and emerging growth company audits
questions.question: Suppose the PCAOB adopts a rule requiring auditors to add an auditor discussion and analysis to their reports. Under Section 103(a)(3)(C), how would it apply to an emerging growth company's audit?

options.A: It would apply to every issuer audit once the SEC approves it
options.B: It would never apply to such audits, whatever the SEC determines
options.C: It would apply if the SEC later decides such audits need it
options.D: It would not apply until the company first needs a 404(b) attestation

questions.key_concept: Board rules on firm rotation or auditor discussion and analysis never apply to emerging growth company audits; other new rules need an SEC determination.
questions.pre_read: Check whether the rule is one of the two kinds the Act names, or some other new rule.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 103(a)(3)(C) treats two kinds of Board rule differently. Rules requiring mandatory audit firm rotation or an auditor discussion and analysis supplement shall not apply to an emerging growth company audit at all; the SEC's power to extend new rules to emerging growth company audits covers other rules adopted after April 5, 2012. Option C is close because it describes that second route, which does not reach this rule.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because SEC approval makes Board rules effective. But Section 103(a)(3)(C) keeps this kind of rule away from emerging growth company audits even after approval.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: an SEC determination can extend other post-2012 rules to emerging growth company audits, but the Act carves auditor discussion and analysis rules out without that option.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because emerging growth companies are exempt from 404(b) attestation. But the Act does not tie this carve-out to 404(b); the rule does not reach their audits.

tips: Eliminate: A treats SEC approval as enough for emerging growth company audits, and D ties the carve-out to the 404(b) attestation, which the Act does not do.
Final two: B beats C because the SEC's determination power covers other post-2012 rules; firm rotation and auditor discussion and analysis rules do not apply to emerging growth company audits.
Exam cue: read Section 103(a)(3)(C) in two parts: two named kinds of rule are out entirely for emerging growth company audits, and other new rules need an SEC decision.

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Accounting standards and PCAOB rulemaking. Changing an existing Board rule
questions.question: The SEC concludes that one of the PCAOB's existing rules no longer conforms to Title I, and the Board declines to change it. Under Section 107(b)(5), what may the SEC do?

options.A: Ask Congress to amend the Board's rule through new legislation
options.B: Direct registered firms to stop following the rule at once
options.C: Amend the Board's rule itself through notice-and-comment rulemaking
options.D: Request a new proposal, since the Board must write any change

questions.key_concept: Under Section 107(b)(5), the SEC may itself amend PCAOB rules by notice-and-comment rulemaking.
questions.pre_read: Ask which body sits above the Board on rules, and how that body must act.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 107(b)(5) applies Exchange Act Section 19(c) to Board rules, so the SEC may by rule abrogate, add to or delete from them to ensure the Board's fair administration, conform its rules to Title I or otherwise further the Act. The SEC publishes notice, takes comment and states its reasons. Option D is close because the Board normally proposes its own rules, but the SEC need not wait for it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because Congress wrote Title I. But the Act already gives the SEC power to amend Board rules; no new law is needed.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the SEC oversees the Board. But it changes a Board rule through rulemaking with notice and comment, not by telling firms to ignore it.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the Board normally proposes its own rules, but Section 107(b)(5) lets the SEC amend a Board rule itself, by notice-and-comment rulemaking.

tips: Eliminate: A sends a rule change to Congress, though the Act gives the SEC that power, and B skips the rulemaking steps the SEC must follow.
Final two: C beats D because Section 107(b)(5) lets the SEC abrogate, add to or delete from Board rules itself; it need not wait for a Board proposal.
Exam cue: the SEC has the last word on PCAOB rules: it approves new ones and can amend existing ones by its own rulemaking.

questions.subtopic: 2B1 Prohibited services and preapproval. Telling investors about approvals
questions.question: An issuer's audit committee preapproved its independent auditor's tax planning work for the year. Under Section 202, how must investors learn of that approval?

options.A: Through disclosure in the issuer's periodic reports filed with the SEC
options.B: Through a Form 8-K current report filed within four business days
options.C: Through a paragraph in the auditor's report on the financial statements
options.D: Through the PCAOB's next public inspection report on the audit firm

questions.key_concept: An audit committee's approval of non-audit services by the auditor is disclosed to investors in the issuer's periodic reports.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose disclosure duty this is, and which kind of SEC report carries it.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 202 adds Exchange Act Section 10A(i)(2): an audit committee's approval of a non-audit service by the issuer's auditor must be disclosed to investors in the periodic reports filed under Section 13(a). Tax planning is not on the Section 201 list, so once preapproved it may proceed, and the approval goes into those reports. Option B is close because Form 8-K covers current events, but the Act puts this disclosure in periodic reports.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: Form 8-K reports specified current events within four business days, but Section 10A(i)(2) places preapproval disclosure in the periodic reports.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the auditor's report goes to investors. But the disclosure duty belongs to the issuer, in its own periodic reports, not to the auditor's opinion.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because PCAOB inspection reports are partly public. But they assess the audit firm; they are not how an issuer discloses its committee's approvals.

tips: Eliminate: C puts the issuer's disclosure in the auditor's opinion, and D in a PCAOB inspection report; the duty is the issuer's own.
Final two: A beats B because Section 10A(i)(2) requires disclosure of non-audit approvals in periodic reports, not in a Form 8-K current report.
Exam cue: auditor non-audit services take two steps: the audit committee preapproves, then the issuer discloses the approval in its periodic reports.

questions.subtopic: 2B1 Prohibited services and preapproval. Exceptions for a listed service
questions.question: An issuer's audit committee wants its independent auditor to act as underwriter on a bond offering and offers to preapprove the engagement. Under Section 201, what route, if any, could permit it?

options.A: Audit committee preapproval, disclosed in the next periodic report
options.B: The de minimis exception, if the fees stay small enough
options.C: Shareholder ratification of the engagement at the annual meeting
options.D: A case-by-case exemption from the PCAOB, subject to SEC review

questions.key_concept: A prohibited non-audit service can be permitted only by a case-by-case PCAOB exemption, subject to SEC review.
questions.pre_read: First decide which kind of service underwriting is, then ask who, if anyone, can make an exception.
questions.correct_explanation: Underwriting for an audit client is an investment banking service that Section 201 bars during the audit, and preapproval cannot cure it. Section 201(b) is the only route: a case-by-case Board exemption, in the public interest and consistent with investor protection, subject to SEC review. It lifts only the statutory ban; SEC Rule 2-01(c)(4)(viii) separately treats underwriting as impairing independence. Option A is close, but preapproval covers only permitted services.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: preapproval and disclosure govern permitted non-audit services such as tax work; a service on the Section 201 list stays barred whatever the committee approves.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the de minimis exception waives preapproval for small services. But it never makes a prohibited service lawful, and this one was recognized at engagement.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because shareholders often ratify the auditor's appointment. But ratification has no role in Section 201 and cannot lift a statutory ban.

tips: Eliminate: B stretches the de minimis waiver to a banned service, and C gives shareholders a power the Act does not; neither can lift a Section 201 ban.
Final two: D beats A because only a case-by-case Board exemption under Section 201(b), reviewed by the SEC, can permit a listed service; preapproval cannot.
Exam cue: a service on the Section 201 list? Preapproval and the de minimis rule do not help; look for a Board exemption.
