questions.subtopic: 2B2 Partner rotation and auditor reports to the audit committee. Returning after rotation
questions.question: Jordan served as lead audit partner on an issuer's audit for the longest consecutive term the rule allows, then rotated off. Under Rule 2-01(c)(6), when may Jordan next serve as that issuer's lead partner?

options.A: After a two-year time-out, like other audit partners
options.B: After a five-year time-out from the lead and reviewing roles
options.C: After a one-year break, matching the cooling-off period
options.D: Never again, since rotating off an audit is permanent

questions.key_concept: A lead partner who rotates off after five years must sit out five years before leading that issuer's audit again.
questions.pre_read: Note Jordan's role and how long Jordan served before rotating off.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 2-01(c)(6) limits a lead partner or engagement quality reviewer to five consecutive years and then bars that partner from either role for that client for the next five consecutive years. Jordan may return as lead partner only after that five-year time-out. Option A is close because other audit partners sit out two years after seven, but that shorter time-out does not apply to lead partners.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a two-year time-out applies to other audit partners after seven years; lead partners and engagement quality reviewers sit out five years.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because Section 206 uses a one-year period. But that period governs hiring audit staff into client finance roles, not a partner's return after rotation.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because rotation sounds final. But the SEC rule sets a five-year time-out, after which the partner may serve that client again.

tips: Eliminate: C borrows Section 206's one-year cooling-off period, and D makes rotation permanent, though the SEC rule sets a fixed time-out.
Final two: B beats A because lead partners and engagement quality reviewers sit out five years under Rule 2-01(c)(6); the two-year time-out is for other audit partners.
Exam cue: partner rotation numbers come in pairs: lead and reviewing partners five on, five off; other audit partners seven on, two off.

questions.subtopic: 2B2 Partner rotation and auditor reports to the audit committee. Timing of reports to the committee
questions.question: Under Rule 2-07, the independent auditor of a listed manufacturer must give the audit committee its Section 204 reports on critical accounting policies and alternative treatments:

options.A: within 90 days after the audit report is filed with the SEC
options.B: whenever the CFO asks the firm to brief the audit committee
options.C: before the audit report on the company is filed with the SEC
options.D: once a year, inside the audit report that shareholders receive

questions.key_concept: The auditor's Section 204 reports reach the audit committee before the audit report is filed with the SEC.
questions.pre_read: Note who receives the reports, then place them in time relative to the audit report.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 204 requires the auditor to report critical accounting policies, alternative GAAP treatments discussed with management and other material written communications to the audit committee on time. SEC Rule 2-07(a) fixes the timing: before the audit report is filed with the SEC. Option A is close because Rule 2-07 mentions a 90-day window, but that is for registered investment companies, and it falls before filing, not after.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: Rule 2-07's 90-day window is for registered investment company updates before filing; for this issuer the reports must come before the audit report is filed.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the CFO manages daily contact with the auditor. But Section 204 makes the auditor report directly and on time, not when management asks.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the audit report goes to shareholders. But Section 204 reports go privately to the audit committee, not into the published audit report.

tips: Eliminate: B makes the reports depend on the CFO, and D publishes them in the audit report; Section 204 reports go directly to the audit committee.
Final two: C beats A because Rule 2-07(a) requires the reports before the audit report is filed; the 90-day window is a registered investment company rule.
Exam cue: Section 204 reports go to the audit committee, before filing; reports routed through the CFO or made after filing are traps.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Conflicts of interest, studies and state regulators. Standards for firms outside the Board
questions.question: Under Section 209, when a state board of accountancy supervises accounting firms that are not registered with the PCAOB, it should:

options.A: apply the PCAOB's issuer audit standards to every firm it licenses
options.B: adopt standards that the SEC has first approved for those firms
options.C: decide the proper standards itself, weighing firm and client size
options.D: apply PCAOB standards to medium-sized firms and its own to small ones

questions.key_concept: State regulators set standards for nonregistered firms independently; PCAOB standards are not presumed to apply to small and medium-sized ones.
questions.pre_read: Note that the firms are not registered, then ask what Title II expects their supervisors to do.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 209 says state regulators supervising nonregistered firms should make an independent determination of the proper standards, weighing the size and nature of the firms' business and of their clients' business. It adds that the Board's standards should not be presumed to apply to small and medium-sized nonregistered firms. Option D is close, but it presumes PCAOB standards for medium-sized firms, which Section 209 rejects.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because PCAOB standards are the benchmark for issuer audits. But Section 209 asks states to decide for themselves rather than extend them to every licensee.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the SEC approves PCAOB rules. But Section 209 gives the SEC no role in approving state standards for nonregistered firms.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: Section 209 says PCAOB standards should not be presumed to apply to small or medium-sized nonregistered firms, so medium-sized firms get no presumption either.

tips: Eliminate: A extends PCAOB standards to every licensee, and B adds SEC approval of state rules; Section 209 leaves the choice to the states.
Final two: C beats D because Section 209 warns against presuming PCAOB standards for small and medium-sized nonregistered firms alike.
Exam cue: registered firms answer to the PCAOB; nonregistered firms answer to state regulators, who choose standards suited to their size and clients.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Conflicts of interest, studies and state regulators. Issuer without an audit committee
questions.question: Lakeview Credit, a Section 15(d) filer with no listed securities and no audit committee, wants its independent auditor to do tax compliance work. Who must preapprove the work under Section 202?

options.A: The full board, which the Act treats as the audit committee
options.B: No one, as preapproval needs an audit committee to exist
options.C: The CFO, who manages the company's relationship with its auditor
options.D: The shareholders, by a vote at the next annual meeting

questions.key_concept: If an issuer has no audit committee, its entire board of directors is the audit committee for Title II duties.
questions.pre_read: Note what Lakeview lacks, then ask whether the Act fills that gap or removes the duty.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 205(a) added an audit committee definition to the Exchange Act: a board committee that oversees accounting, financial reporting and audits or, if no such committee exists, the entire board of directors. So Section 202's preapproval duty falls on Lakeview's full board. Option B is close because Lakeview has no committee, but the definition fills that gap rather than removing the duty.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: Lakeview has no committee, but Section 205(a) defines the audit committee as the entire board when none exists, so preapproval is still required.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the CFO works with the auditor daily. But preapproval belongs to the audit committee, here the whole board, and never to management.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because shareholders often ratify the auditor's appointment. But Section 202 gives preapproval of services to the audit committee, not to shareholders.

tips: Eliminate: C hands preapproval to management, and D to shareholders; Section 202 gives it to the audit committee.
Final two: A beats B because Section 205(a) treats the entire board as the audit committee when an issuer has none, so the preapproval duty remains.
Exam cue: no audit committee in the stem? Under the Exchange Act definition, the whole board takes on the audit committee's duties.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Conflicts of interest, studies and state regulators. Consequence of a barred service
questions.question: When a registered firm provides an issuer with a non-audit service that Section 201 prohibits, Section 208(b) makes it unlawful for the firm to:

options.A: bill the issuer for the service until its audit committee ratifies it
options.B: keep its PCAOB registration for the rest of that fiscal year
options.C: audit any other issuer until the SEC lifts the restriction
options.D: prepare or issue any audit report with respect to that issuer

questions.key_concept: Section 208(b) makes it unlawful for a firm to issue an issuer's audit report after a prohibited activity with that issuer.
questions.pre_read: Ask what Title II ties the consequence to: the firm, the service or the issuer it served.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 208(b) makes it unlawful for a registered firm, or an associated person, to prepare or issue any audit report for an issuer if it engages in an activity with that issuer that Exchange Act Section 10A(g) to (l), or SEC or Board rules under them, prohibit. A banned service therefore stops the firm from reporting on that issuer. Option C is close but overreaches: the bar applies issuer by issuer.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the audit committee approves permitted services. But approval cannot cure a prohibited service, and Section 208(b) targets the audit report.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the PCAOB can revoke registration. But revocation needs a disciplinary proceeding under Section 105; Section 208(b) makes the audit report unlawful.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the consequence is serious, but Section 208(b) ties it to the issuer that received the barred service, not to the firm's other issuer audits.

tips: Eliminate: A treats audit committee approval as a cure, and B makes loss of registration automatic, though revocation needs a Board disciplinary proceeding.
Final two: D beats C because Section 208(b) makes the audit report for that issuer unlawful; it does not stop the firm's audits of other issuers.
Exam cue: a Title II independence breach is measured issuer by issuer: the firm may not report on the client it compromised.

questions.subtopic: 2A1 Establishment, funding and SEC oversight. Limits on Board service
questions.question: The SEC is filling a PCAOB seat and is considering a former Board member who served two full five-year terms, years apart. Under Section 101(e)(5), this candidate:

options.A: may serve as chairperson, since the chair has its own term limit
options.B: may serve again as a member, as the terms were not consecutive
options.C: may not serve again, whether as a member or as chairperson
options.D: may not return until a full term has passed since the last

questions.key_concept: No one may serve as a PCAOB member, or as its chairperson, for more than two terms, consecutive or not (Section 101(e)(5)(B)).
questions.pre_read: Recall the limits Section 101(e) places on how long one person may serve on the Board.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 101(e)(5)(B) says no person may serve as a Board member, or as chairperson, for more than two terms, whether or not the terms are consecutive. Two full terms therefore end this candidate's eligibility for any seat on the Board. Option B is the closest misreading: the gap between the terms does not matter, because the statute counts terms, not consecutive years.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the chair is a distinct role. But Section 101(e)(5)(B) applies the same two-term limit to service as a member or as chairperson.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a gap between terms looks like a fresh start, but the limit applies whether or not the two terms were consecutive.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because some term limits allow a return after a break. Section 101(e)(5)(B) sets no waiting period; the two-term cap is permanent.

tips: Eliminate: A gives the chair a separate limit, though one two-term cap covers member and chair, and D adds a waiting period the Act does not contain.
Final two: C beats B because Section 101(e)(5)(B) counts terms whether or not they are consecutive, so a gap does not reset the count.
Exam cue: for PCAOB seats, count terms, not years in a row: a gap between terms never resets the two-term cap.

questions.subtopic: 2A1 Establishment, funding and SEC oversight. When the Board itself falls short
questions.question: After notice and a hearing, the SEC finds on the record that the PCAOB, without reasonable justification, failed to enforce its standards against a registered firm. Under Section 107(d), what may the SEC do?

options.A: Censure the Board or impose limits on its activities and operations
options.B: Censure individual members, as the Board as a body cannot be sanctioned
options.C: Impose a civil money penalty on the Board, paid to the Treasury
options.D: Ask Congress to dissolve the Board, as no other remedy reaches it

questions.key_concept: Under Section 107(d)(2), the SEC may censure the PCAOB or limit its activities after notice and a hearing.
questions.pre_read: Recall the SEC's oversight tools under Section 107 and whom each one reaches.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 107(d)(2) lets the SEC, by order after notice and a hearing, censure the PCAOB or limit its activities, functions and operations when it finds the Board failed, without reasonable justification, to enforce compliance. Section 107(d)(1) also lets the SEC relieve the Board of enforcement duties by rule. Option B is close: Section 107(d)(3) reaches individual members, but it does not replace the remedy against the Board itself.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: Section 107(d)(3) lets the SEC censure or remove individual members, but Section 107(d)(2) also reaches the Board as a body.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the SEC can seek money penalties against others. Section 107(d) gives it censure and limits on the Board, not fines.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the Board lasts until Congress dissolves it. But Section 107(d) gives the SEC its own remedies, so no act of Congress is needed.

tips: Eliminate: C treats the Board like a firm facing money penalties, and D sends the SEC to Congress, though Section 107(d) gives the SEC its own remedies.
Final two: A beats B because Section 107(d)(2) reaches the Board as a body; the member-level power in Section 107(d)(3) sits beside it.
Exam cue: the SEC oversees the PCAOB at three levels: its rules, its sanctions on firms, and the Board and its members.

questions.subtopic: 2A2 Registration and foreign audit firms. Refused registration
questions.question: The PCAOB sends a written notice of disapproval on an audit firm's completed registration application, and the firm believes the Board misread its quality control policies. Under Section 102(c)(2), what recourse does the firm have?

options.A: None, since the Board's registration decisions are final when issued
options.B: It may simply refile, since the Board must decide in 45 days
options.C: It may ask the Board to reconsider; the SEC has no role
options.D: It may seek SEC review, since the refusal counts as a sanction

questions.key_concept: A PCAOB disapproval of a registration application is treated as a disciplinary sanction, so the SEC can review it (Section 102(c)(2)).
questions.pre_read: Decide how the Act classifies a registration refusal, then recall what follows for any action in that class.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 102(c)(2) treats a written notice of disapproval of a completed application as a disciplinary sanction for the purposes of Sections 105(d) and 107(c). Like any final Board sanction, it is reported and open to SEC review, the Act's remedy for contesting it; refiling only starts a new application. Option C is close because the Board decides first, but saying the SEC has no role misses Section 107(c).

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the Board approves or disapproves applications itself. But Section 102(c)(2) makes a disapproval a sanction, and Board sanctions are subject to SEC review.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because Section 102(c)(1) sets a 45-day clock. That clock governs the Board's decision on a completed application; it is not an appeal route.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the Board makes the first decision, but Section 102(c)(2) brings a disapproval within Section 107(c), so the SEC can review it.

tips: Eliminate: A makes the Board's decision final, though its sanctions go to the SEC for review, and B turns the 45-day decision deadline into a remedy.
Final two: D beats C because Section 102(c)(2) treats a disapproval as a disciplinary sanction, which brings in SEC review under Section 107(c).
Exam cue: when the Act says a Board action is 'treated as a disciplinary sanction', think SEC review and public reporting.

questions.subtopic: 2A2 Registration and foreign audit firms. Public access to registration filings
questions.question: When registering with the PCAOB, an audit firm reasonably identifies detailed parts of its quality control manual as proprietary. Under Section 102(e), what must the Board do with those parts?

options.A: Publish them with the rest of the application for public inspection
options.B: Protect them from public disclosure, though the rest may be public
options.C: Send them to state boards, which decide whether to publish them
options.D: Withhold them once the SEC confirms that they are proprietary

questions.key_concept: Registration filings are open to public inspection, but the Board must protect information a firm reasonably identifies as proprietary (Section 102(e)).
questions.pre_read: Look for the default rule on registration filings, then for the exception a firm can invoke.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 102(e) makes registration applications and annual reports available for public inspection, subject to Board and SEC rules and confidentiality laws, but says that in all events the Board shall protect from public disclosure information the firm reasonably identifies as proprietary. The duty sits with the Board and needs no SEC finding. Option D is close, yet it adds an SEC step the section does not require.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because Section 102(e) does open applications to public inspection. But it carves out information the firm reasonably identifies as proprietary.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because state boards license accounting firms. But Section 102(e) gives the duty to protect proprietary registration information to the Board itself.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the SEC can write rules on public availability, but Section 102(e) says the Board protects reasonably identified proprietary information in all events, with no SEC finding needed.

tips: Eliminate: A publishes material the firm reasonably marked proprietary, and C hands the decision to state boards, though Section 102(e) gives the Board the duty.
Final two: B beats D because Section 102(e) requires the Board to protect reasonably identified proprietary information in all events, without first getting an SEC finding.
Exam cue: registration filings are public by default, but proprietary parts the firm reasonably flags stay protected.

questions.subtopic: 2A2 Registration and foreign audit firms. A foreign firm behind the fieldwork
questions.question: A Singapore accounting firm signs no audit reports but performs most of the fieldwork for a registered firm's audits of several issuers. Under Section 106(a)(2), what may the PCAOB do?

options.A: Nothing, as firms that sign no audit reports are outside the Act
options.B: Obtain its workpapers on request, but not require it to register
options.C: Require it, by rule, to register and accept the Board's oversight
options.D: Register it once Singapore's audit regulator has given consent

questions.key_concept: The Board may, by rule, require a foreign firm with a substantial role in issuer audits to register and accept its oversight (Section 106(a)(2)).
questions.pre_read: Note what the foreign firm does and does not do, then recall which part of Section 106 reaches it.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 106(a)(2) lets the Board determine, by rule, that a foreign firm which issues no audit reports but plays a substantial role in preparing them for particular issuers is treated as a public accounting firm for registration and Board oversight. Option B is close: the firm's workpapers are reachable under Section 106(b), but that does not exhaust the Board's power over a substantial-role firm.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because registration attaches to firms that issue audit reports. Section 106(a)(2) extends it, by Board rule, to foreign firms with a substantial role.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a foreign firm whose material work is relied on must produce workpapers under Section 106(b), but Section 106(a)(2) also allows required registration.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because foreign regulators matter for inspections. But registration with the PCAOB is the Board's decision under Section 106(a)(2), not the home regulator's.

tips: Eliminate: A limits the Act to report signers, though Section 106(a)(2) reaches substantial contributors, and D makes PCAOB registration depend on a foreign regulator's consent.
Final two: C beats B because Section 106(a)(2) lets the Board, by rule, require registration and oversight of a substantial-role firm, beyond producing workpapers.
Exam cue: signing an issuer's audit report means registering; a substantial role without signing can mean registering too, once the Board says so by rule.

questions.subtopic: 2A2 Registration and foreign audit firms. Exempting foreign firms
questions.question: Under Section 106(c), a foreign public accounting firm, or a class of such firms, may be exempted from provisions of the Act or the rules under it by:

options.A: the SEC, or the PCAOB acting with the SEC's approval
options.B: the PCAOB alone, as the body that registers firms
options.C: its home-country regulator, under a mutual recognition deal
options.D: the issuer's audit committee, for that issuer's audits

questions.key_concept: The SEC, or the PCAOB with the SEC's approval, may exempt a foreign firm or class of firms from the Act (Section 106(c)).
questions.pre_read: Identify which bodies Section 106 lets relax its rules for foreign firms, and whether one needs another's approval.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 106(c) lets the SEC, and the Board subject to the SEC's approval, exempt any foreign public accounting firm or class of firms from any provision of the Act or of Board or SEC rules, by rule, regulation or order, either unconditionally or on stated terms. Option B is close, but the Board cannot grant such an exemption without the SEC's approval.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the Board does register and oversee foreign firms, but under Section 106(c) any exemption it grants needs the SEC's approval.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because cooperation with foreign regulators matters. But Section 106(c) leaves exemptions to U.S. authorities; a home regulator cannot exempt a firm from the Act.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the audit committee oversees the auditor. It has no power to exempt any firm from the Act or the Board's rules.

tips: Eliminate: C hands the exemption to a foreign regulator and D to the audit committee, though Section 106(c) names only the SEC and the Board.
Final two: A beats B because Section 106(c) requires the SEC's approval for any exemption the Board grants to a foreign firm.

questions.subtopic: 2A2 Registration and foreign audit firms. Producing papers from abroad
questions.question: The PCAOB requests workpapers from a German firm whose audit work a registered firm relied on, but German law hinders direct transfer. Under Section 106(f), how may the German firm comply?

options.A: It need not respond, since German law overrides a U.S. request
options.B: It may wait for a U.S. court order before producing anything
options.C: By direct production alone, as the Act allows no other route
options.D: Through alternate means staff allow, such as German regulators

questions.key_concept: Under Section 106(f), staff may let a foreign firm meet its production duty through alternate means, such as foreign counterpart regulators.
questions.pre_read: Recall what Section 106 says about producing papers when foreign law gets in the way.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 106(f), added by Dodd-Frank in 2010, lets SEC or Board staff allow a foreign firm subject to Section 106 to meet its production obligations through alternate means, such as through the SEC's or the Board's foreign counterparts. The duty to produce remains; only the channel changes. Option C is close, but it overlooks that statutory flexibility.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because foreign law can block transfers. But Section 106 still subjects the firm to production duties; home-country law does not cancel them.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because U.S. courts can enforce these requests under Section 106(b). But a willful refusal is itself a violation of the Act under Section 106(e).
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: production is mandatory, but Section 106(f) lets staff accept an alternate channel, such as a foreign counterpart regulator.

tips: Eliminate: A lets foreign law cancel the duty, and B treats a court order as a precondition, though a willful refusal violates the Act under Section 106(e).
Final two: D beats C because Section 106(f) lets staff allow alternate means, such as foreign counterparts, to satisfy the same production duty.
Exam cue: for foreign workpapers, the duty to produce is fixed, but the route can run through a foreign regulator.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Standards, inspections and discipline. Internal control testing in the report
questions.question: For a large accelerated filer, Section 103(a)(2)(A)(iii) requires the PCAOB's auditing standards to make the independent auditor:

options.A: certify internal control is effective on management's behalf
options.B: describe its internal control testing scope in the audit report
options.C: give an opinion on the issuer's disclosure controls and procedures
options.D: report control weaknesses to the audit committee, not in the report

questions.key_concept: Board standards must make each issuer audit report describe the auditor's internal control testing and present its findings (Section 103(a)(2)(A)(iii)).
questions.pre_read: Ask where the Act wants the auditor's internal control work to appear, and what it must contain.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 103(a)(2)(A)(iii) requires Board auditing standards to make each issuer audit report describe the scope of the auditor's testing of internal control under Section 404(b), and present, in that report or a separate one, the findings, an evaluation of the controls and, at a minimum, any material weaknesses. Option D is close, but the description belongs in the report, not only in a committee briefing.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the auditor reports on internal control. But the auditor attests; management assesses ICFR and the officers certify, so the auditor certifies nothing for management.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because officers evaluate disclosure controls under Section 302. Section 103 points the auditor at internal control over financial reporting, tested under Section 404(b).
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the audit committee does hear from the auditor, but Section 103 puts the testing scope, findings and material weaknesses in the audit report or a separate report.

tips: Eliminate: A has the auditor certify for management, though management assesses and officers certify, and C swaps in disclosure controls, which Section 302 assigns to the officers.
Final two: B beats D because Section 103(a)(2)(A)(iii) puts the testing scope and findings in the audit report itself, or a separate report, not only in a committee briefing.
Exam cue: when an option moves a required statement out of the audit report into a private briefing, check whether the Act places it in the report.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Standards, inspections and discipline. Supervisors and a team member's breach
questions.question: A manager breached PCAOB standards, though firm procedures met Board rules and could reasonably catch breaches, and the supervising partner reasonably applied them without cause for doubt. Under Section 105(c)(6), what follows for the partner?

options.A: The partner is not deemed to have failed to supervise the manager
options.B: The partner may be sanctioned, since any breach shows weak supervision
options.C: The partner is protected, but the Board must then sanction the firm
options.D: The partner shares the manager's sanction automatically as supervisor

questions.key_concept: A supervisor who reasonably followed compliant firm procedures, with no cause for suspicion, has not failed to supervise (Section 105(c)(6)(B)).
questions.pre_read: Note what the firm had in place and how the partner behaved, then recall the conditions of the supervision rule.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 105(c)(6)(A) lets the Board sanction a firm, or a supervisory person, for failing reasonably to supervise someone who then breaks the rules. Under Section 105(c)(6)(B), no supervisor has failed if the firm had compliant procedures reasonably expected to prevent and detect the violation, and the supervisor reasonably carried them out with no cause to suspect noncompliance. Option B overlooks that protection.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a breach can lead to supervision sanctions, but Section 105(c)(6)(B) shields a supervisor who reasonably followed compliant procedures without cause for suspicion.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the firm sets the procedures. But nothing in Section 105(c)(6) makes a sanction on the firm automatic, and here its compliant procedures help protect the partner.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because supervisors answer for their teams. Section 105(c)(6) has no automatic sharing of sanctions; it requires a failure reasonably to supervise.

tips: Eliminate: C makes a sanction on the firm mandatory and D makes the supervisor share the manager's sanction; Section 105(c)(6) imposes neither result automatically.
Final two: A beats B because Section 105(c)(6)(B) protects a supervisor who reasonably followed compliant procedures and had no reasonable cause for suspicion.
Exam cue: in supervision items, check two facts: compliant procedures existed, and the supervisor reasonably followed them. Both together mean no failure to supervise.

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Accounting standards and PCAOB rulemaking. Who may govern a standard setter
questions.question: A private standard setter seeks SEC recognition of its accounting principles under Section 108, and most of its trustees are current partners at registered audit firms. Which criterion does the body fail?

options.A: It must be organized as a government body under SEC control
options.B: Its trustees must be named by the SEC after consulting the Treasury
options.C: A trustee majority must have no recent or present audit firm ties
options.D: It must be funded by contributions from the audit firms it affects

questions.key_concept: A recognized standard setter needs a trustee majority not tied to registered audit firms now or in the prior two years (Section 108).
questions.pre_read: Match the fact about the trustees to the governance criteria Section 108 sets for a standard setter.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 108, adding Securities Act Section 19(b), lets the SEC recognize principles only from a private body whose board of trustees, serving the public interest, has a majority who are not, and in the two years before service were not, associated persons of a registered firm. Trustees who are current audit firm partners break that test. Option B borrows the PCAOB's appointment process, which Section 108 does not impose.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the SEC oversees recognition. But Section 108 requires the standard setter to be organized as a private entity, not a government body.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the SEC appoints PCAOB members after consulting the Treasury Secretary, but Section 108 sets no appointment rule for a standard setter's trustees.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because firms rely on the standards. Section 108 requires funding under Section 109, through accounting support fees, not contributions from the audit firms.

tips: Eliminate: A makes the body governmental, though Section 108 requires a private entity, and D relies on firm contributions, though funding must come under Section 109.
Final two: C beats B because Section 108's governance test is a trustee majority free of registered firm ties; the SEC appointment process belongs to the PCAOB.
Exam cue: Section 108 recognition rests on independence from the audit profession: a private body, independent trustees, Section 109 funding and prompt majority-vote updates.

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Accounting standards and PCAOB rulemaking. Study of principles-based accounting
questions.question: A finance director researching U.S. debates on principles-based accounting reads Section 108(d). Which body did that section direct to study adopting a principles-based accounting system?

options.A: FASB, as the private standard setter that writes the principles
options.B: The PCAOB, through its standard-setting advisory groups
options.C: The Treasury Secretary, with the Federal Reserve chair
options.D: The SEC, which then had to report its findings to Congress

questions.key_concept: Section 108(d) required the SEC to study adopting a principles-based accounting system and report its results to Congress within one year.
questions.pre_read: Recall which bodies the Act gives accounting tasks and which it gives auditing tasks.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 108(d) directed the SEC to study the adoption of a principles-based accounting system in the United States, covering how far one already existed, how long a change would take, how it could be implemented and its economic effects, and to report to the Senate Banking and House Financial Services Committees within one year. Option A is close, since FASB writes the standards, but the study was the SEC's task.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: FASB writes U.S. accounting standards, but Section 108(d) gave the study of a principles-based system to the SEC.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the PCAOB convenes advisory groups on standards. Those groups work on auditing and related standards, not accounting principles, and Section 108(d) names the SEC.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because both officials are consulted before PCAOB appointments. Neither was given the principles-based accounting study under Section 108(d).

tips: Eliminate: B gives an accounting study to the auditing standard setter, and C borrows the two officials consulted on PCAOB appointments.
Final two: D beats A because Section 108(d) assigned the study to the SEC, whose own power to set accounting principles Section 108(c) preserves.
Exam cue: for each study the Act orders, tie the subject to its overseer: an accounting-system question went to the SEC, not to the PCAOB or FASB.

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Accounting standards and PCAOB rulemaking. Standards drawn from professional groups
questions.question: Years ago the PCAOB adopted, as its own rules, parts of auditing standards proposed by a professional group of accountants. Under Section 103(a)(3)(A), who may now amend or repeal those parts?

options.A: The professional group that originally proposed them
options.B: The Board, which keeps full authority over what it adopts
options.C: Each registered firm, for its own audits, by written policy
options.D: State boards of accountancy, which license the firms using them

questions.key_concept: Standards the PCAOB adopts from professional groups become Board rules, and the Board keeps full authority to amend or repeal them.
questions.pre_read: Recall what Section 103 says about standards the Board takes from outside groups.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 103(a)(3)(A)(i) lets the Board adopt as its rules any portion of professional standards proposed by designated professional groups or by its own advisory groups, and clause (ii) says the Board keeps full authority to modify, supplement, revise, amend or repeal them, in whole or in part. Once adopted, they are Board rules. Option A is close, but the proposing group has no power over the Board's rules.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the group wrote the original text, but once the Board adopts it, Section 103(a)(3)(A)(ii) gives the Board full authority to change or repeal it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because firms tailor their audit methodology. But they must follow Board standards as written; no firm can amend or repeal a Board rule by its own policy.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because states license accountants. But a state board cannot amend PCAOB rules; the Act gives that power to the Board.

tips: Eliminate: C lets each firm rewrite Board rules by policy, and D gives state licensing boards power over PCAOB standards, which the Act does not.
Final two: B beats A because Section 103(a)(3)(A)(ii) keeps full authority with the Board to amend or repeal standards it adopted from a professional group.
Exam cue: once the PCAOB adopts a standard, its origin no longer matters: it is a Board rule, and the group that proposed it keeps no say over it.

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Accounting standards and PCAOB rulemaking. Who may advise on standards
questions.question: An investor advocate objects that practicing accountants serve on a PCAOB expert advisory group drafting a proposed auditing standard. Under Section 103(a)(4), which statement is accurate?

options.A: They may serve, subject to Board rules preventing conflicts of interest
options.B: They may not serve, as Board members may not practice accounting either
options.C: They may serve, and the group's draft binds the Board once delivered
options.D: They may not serve unless the SEC approves each of their appointments

questions.key_concept: PCAOB expert advisory groups may include practicing accountants, subject to Board conflict-of-interest rules, and they make recommendations on standards.
questions.pre_read: Recall what Section 103 says about who may sit on the Board's advisory groups.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 103(a)(4) requires the Board to convene, or let its staff convene, expert advisory groups that may include practicing accountants and other experts, as well as representatives of other interested groups, subject to Board rules to prevent conflicts of interest. The groups recommend content, including draft standards. Option B is close, but the full-time, no-practice rule in Section 101(e) binds Board members, not advisory group participants.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: Section 101(e) bars Board members from practicing accounting, but Section 103(a)(4) expressly allows practicing accountants on advisory groups, under conflict-of-interest rules.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the groups may draft proposals. But they make recommendations; the Board decides what, if anything, to adopt as its own rule.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the SEC oversees the Board. But Section 103(a)(4) leaves convening advisory groups to the Board or its staff, with no SEC sign-off on members.

tips: Eliminate: C makes an advisory draft binding, though the groups only recommend, and D adds SEC approval of members, which Section 103(a)(4) does not require.
Final two: A beats B because Section 103(a)(4) lets practicing accountants serve on advisory groups under conflict rules; the no-practice limit binds Board members.
Exam cue: keep apart who sits on the Board and who advises it: limits on Board members do not carry over to its advisers.

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Accounting standards and PCAOB rulemaking. Procedure for a proposed Board rule
questions.question: A governance analyst tracking a draft PCAOB standard learns that Section 107(b)(4) governs how the SEC processes it. The SEC handles the draft as if the Board were:

options.A: a federal agency issuing a rule under the Administrative Procedure Act
options.B: an SEC division whose rules the Chief Accountant signs into effect
options.C: a registered securities association filing a proposed rule change
options.D: a state board of accountancy adopting licensing rules for CPAs

questions.key_concept: Section 107(b)(4) runs proposed PCAOB rules through Exchange Act Section 19(b) as if the Board were a registered securities association.
questions.pre_read: Recall which existing oversight model the Act borrows for the Board's proposed rules.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 107(b)(4) makes paragraphs (1) to (3) of Exchange Act Section 19(b) govern the Board's proposed rules as fully as if the Board were a registered securities association, with Title I's approval standard read into Section 19(b)(2). It is the route used for rule changes of self-regulatory organizations such as FINRA. Option A is close, but the statute names the self-regulatory organization route, not agency rulemaking.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: an agency's rulemaking procedure is the familiar model, but Section 107(b)(4) applies the Exchange Act Section 19(b) process for self-regulatory organizations instead.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the SEC oversees the Board's rules. But Section 107(b)(4) gives no official power to sign a Board rule into effect; the Exchange Act filing process applies.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because states license CPAs. But Section 107(b)(4) borrows Exchange Act procedures; state licensing rulemaking plays no part in Board rules.

tips: Eliminate: B makes the Board an SEC division whose rules an official signs, and D borrows state licensing procedure; Section 107(b)(4) uses the Exchange Act instead.
Final two: C beats A because Section 107(b)(4) applies Exchange Act Section 19(b) as if the Board were a registered securities association, not agency rulemaking procedure.
Exam cue: the PCAOB is overseen like a self-regulatory organization, so its rules move through the Exchange Act Section 19 process.

questions.subtopic: 2B1 Prohibited services and preapproval. A comfort letter for underwriters
questions.question: An issuer's CFO plans to have its independent auditor issue a comfort letter to underwriters, saying audit services need no audit committee action. Under Section 202, which statement is accurate?

options.A: No committee approval is needed, as preapproval covers non-audit work alone
options.B: It is barred, as an investment banking service under Section 201
options.C: The CFO may approve it, as management engages the auditor for audits
options.D: The audit committee must preapprove it, like every audit service

questions.key_concept: The audit committee must preapprove all auditing services, comfort letters included, not only non-audit services (Exchange Act Section 10A(i)(1)(A)).
questions.pre_read: Ask whether preapproval is limited to non-audit work, and how the Act classes a comfort letter.
questions.correct_explanation: Exchange Act Section 10A(i)(1)(A), added by Section 202, requires the audit committee to preapprove all auditing services, which it says may include comfort letters for securities underwritings, as well as permitted non-audit services. Rule 2-01(c)(7) repeats the requirement. Option A is close, but the de minimis waiver applies only to non-audit services; audit services always need approval in advance.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the de minimis waiver covers only non-audit services, but Section 10A(i)(1)(A) requires preapproval of all auditing services, comfort letters included.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because comfort letters relate to underwritings. But the Act lists them among auditing services; the Section 201 ban targets acting as an investment banker.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the CFO manages daily contact with the auditor. But Section 202 gives preapproval to the audit committee, and management cannot stand in for it.

tips: Eliminate: B bans comfort letters, though the Act treats them as auditing services, and C hands approval to the CFO, though Section 202 gives it to the audit committee.
Final two: D beats A because Section 10A(i)(1)(A) requires preapproval of all auditing services; only non-audit services can use the de minimis waiver.
Exam cue: preapproval covers everything the auditor does for the issuer, audit work included; the waiver is only for small, unrecognized non-audit work.

questions.subtopic: 2B2 Partner rotation and auditor reports to the audit committee. Letters to management
questions.question: Midway through an issuer's audit, the independent auditor sends management a letter recommending fixes to internal control weaknesses. Under Section 204, what must the auditor do with that letter?

options.A: Keep it in the audit workpapers, since it was addressed to management
options.B: Report it to the audit committee as a material written communication
options.C: File it with the PCAOB as part of the firm's annual report
options.D: Give it to the committee if management rejects the recommendations

questions.key_concept: Material written communications between the auditor and management, such as a management letter, must also be reported to the audit committee.
questions.pre_read: Recall what Section 204 requires the auditor to share, and with whom.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 204 added Exchange Act Section 10A(k), which requires the auditor to report to the audit committee other material written communications with management, such as a management letter or schedule of unadjusted differences. Rule 2-07(a)(3) repeats this, and the SEC's adopting release lists reports on internal control observations as an example. Option D is close, but the duty does not depend on any dispute.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the letter went to management. But Section 10A(k)(3) exists to pass material auditor-management correspondence on to the audit committee.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because firms file annual reports with the PCAOB. Those cover registration information, not client letters; Section 204 sends this letter to the audit committee.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a dispute makes the letter more urgent, but Section 204 requires reporting material written communications whether or not management agrees.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps the letter in the files, though Section 204 sends material correspondence onward, and C routes it to the PCAOB, which receives firm reports, not client letters.
Final two: B beats D because Section 204 requires the auditor to report material written communications with management to the audit committee, dispute or not.
Exam cue: if the auditor put it in writing to management and it matters, the audit committee gets it too.

questions.subtopic: 2B2 Partner rotation and auditor reports to the audit committee. Rotation at a very small firm
questions.question: A registered firm with six partners and three issuer audit clients has kept the same lead partner on one issuer for seven years. Under Rule 2-01(c)(6)(ii), what keeps the firm independent?

options.A: A PCAOB review of that engagement at least once every three years
options.B: Nothing further; firms this small are exempt from partner rotation outright
options.C: Audit committee approval of the partner's extra years of service
options.D: Moving the lead partner into the engagement quality reviewer role

questions.key_concept: A firm with under five issuer clients and under ten partners skips rotation only while the PCAOB reviews each affected engagement every three years.
questions.pre_read: Recall what the SEC rule asks of very small firms in place of partner rotation.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 2-01(c)(6)(ii) exempts a firm with fewer than five issuer audit clients and fewer than ten partners from the rotation limits, but only if the PCAOB reviews each engagement that would otherwise breach them at least once every three years; the SEC adopted it using its exemptive powers, including Exchange Act Section 36, and calls this a special review. Option B is close, but the exemption carries that condition.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the firm is small enough for the exemption, but Rule 2-01(c)(6)(ii) keeps it only while the PCAOB reviews the engagement at least once every three years.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the audit committee oversees the auditor. But neither Section 203 nor Rule 2-01(c)(6) lets the committee extend a partner's service.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because moving partners between roles looks like rotation. But the time-out after lead service also bars the engagement quality reviewer role.

tips: Eliminate: C gives the audit committee a power to extend partner service that no rule grants, and D moves the partner into a role the rotation time-out also covers.
Final two: A beats B because Rule 2-01(c)(6)(ii) exempts a small firm from rotation only while the PCAOB reviews each affected engagement at least once every three years.
Exam cue: two small-firm exemptions look alike: partner pay rules exempt small firms outright, but rotation relief lasts only while the PCAOB reviews the engagements.

questions.subtopic: 2B2 Partner rotation and auditor reports to the audit committee. A technical adviser to the audit team
questions.question: Over eight straight years, a partner in an audit firm's national office has advised an issuer's audit team on complex revenue questions, without leading or reviewing the audit. Under Rule 2-01(c)(6), what applies?

options.A: The partner must rotate after seven years, like other audit partners
options.B: The partner must rotate after five years, like the lead partner
options.C: No rotation applies, as a consulting partner is not an audit partner
options.D: No rotation applies, since the Act rotates firms, not partners

questions.key_concept: Partners who only consult the audit team on technical or industry issues are not audit partners, so SEC rotation rules do not reach them.
questions.pre_read: Before counting years, check which partners the SEC rotation rule covers.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 2-01(f)(7)(ii) defines an audit partner to exclude a partner who consults with the audit engagement team on technical or industry-specific issues, and the SEC's adopting release confirms that national office partners consulted on client matters are not audit partners. Rotation under Rule 2-01(c)(6) applies only to audit partners, so this partner need not rotate. Option A is close, but it treats the consultant as an audit partner.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: other audit partners do rotate after seven years, but the definition in Rule 2-01(f)(7)(ii) leaves out partners who only consult on technical issues.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because five years is the best-known limit. But that limit is for the partners who lead or review the audit, roles this partner never held.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because firm rotation is often debated. But the Act and SEC rules rotate partners; firm rotation was only studied, never required.

tips: Eliminate: B applies the lead partner's five-year limit to someone who never led or reviewed the audit, and D swaps partner rotation for firm rotation, which no rule requires.
Final two: C beats A because Rule 2-01(f)(7)(ii) excludes technical consulting partners from 'audit partner', so the seven-year limit never reaches them.
Exam cue: before applying a rotation limit, ask whether the person is an audit partner at all: lead, reviewer, or a decision-maker in regular client contact.

questions.subtopic: 2B2 Partner rotation and auditor reports to the audit committee. Partners on a large subsidiary
questions.question: For six years, a partner has led the audit of an issuer's subsidiary holding 30% of consolidated assets, without working at the parent level. Under Rule 2-01(f)(7)(ii), the partner:

options.A: is not an audit partner, as the term stops at parent level
options.B: must rotate off now, as five years is every partner's limit
options.C: is covered if the subsidiary is itself an SEC registrant
options.D: is an audit partner, so the SEC rotation limits apply

questions.key_concept: A lead partner on a subsidiary with 20% or more of consolidated assets or revenues is an audit partner covered by rotation (Rule 2-01(f)(7)(ii)(D)).
questions.pre_read: Recall which partners outside the parent-level team the SEC's definition of audit partner reaches.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 2-01(f)(7)(ii)(D) includes in the definition of audit partner the lead partner on any subsidiary whose assets or revenues are 20% or more of the issuer's consolidated assets or revenues. At 30% of assets this subsidiary passes that test, so the partner is an audit partner and the rotation limits in Rule 2-01(c)(6) apply. Option A is close, but the definition reaches beyond the parent level.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: many audit partners serve at the parent level, but Rule 2-01(f)(7)(ii)(D) adds lead partners on subsidiaries at or above the 20% line.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because five years is the best-known limit. But it binds the lead partner and reviewer; other audit partners get seven years, so six is no breach yet.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the rules concern issuers. But the test looks at the subsidiary's share of consolidated assets or revenues, not at whether it files with the SEC itself.

tips: Eliminate: B gives every audit partner the five-year limit meant for the lead partner and reviewer, and C adds a registrant test the definition does not contain.
Final two: D beats A because Rule 2-01(f)(7)(ii)(D) makes the lead partner on a subsidiary with 20% or more of consolidated assets or revenues an audit partner.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Conflicts of interest, studies and state regulators. A brief stint on the audit
questions.question: Last year an audit associate spent eight hours observing an issuer's inventory count for its audit; the issuer now hires the associate as controller. Under Rule 2-01(c)(2)(iii)(B)(2)(i), what applies to the firm?

options.A: It may not audit the issuer this year; every audit hour counts
options.B: It may keep auditing; ten or fewer hours are not team membership
options.C: It may keep auditing if the audit committee approves the hire
options.D: It may not audit until a new lead partner takes over

questions.key_concept: Under the SEC rule, staff with 10 or fewer audit hours, other than the lead partner and reviewer, do not trigger the cooling-off bar.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each fact in the stem against the SEC rule's version of the cooling-off test.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 2-01(c)(2)(iii)(B) bars the firm when a former audit engagement team member takes a financial reporting oversight role, such as controller, within the one-year look-back. But paragraph (B)(2)(i) excludes from the team anyone, other than the lead partner and engagement quality reviewer, who gave 10 or fewer hours of audit, review or attest services. Eight hours falls below that line. Option A is close, but the SEC rule draws the participation line at 10 hours.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: Section 206 says 'any capacity', but the SEC's adopting release reads 'participated' as more than 10 hours for all but the lead partner and engagement quality reviewer.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the rule has an audit committee route. It is for emergencies or unusual situations, and the hours exclusion already settles this hire.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because rotation brings fresh eyes. But the cooling-off rule turns on the hire's audit work, and changing the lead partner does not cure a covered hire.

tips: Eliminate: C borrows the emergency exception, which is for unusual situations, and D treats partner rotation as a cure for a cooling-off problem.
Final two: B beats A because Rule 2-01(c)(2)(iii)(B) excludes team members with 10 or fewer hours, other than the lead partner and reviewer, from the cooling-off bar.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Conflicts of interest, studies and state regulators. A hire into a role the Act does not name
questions.question: An audit manager who worked throughout an issuer's audit last year joins the issuer as general counsel, a role Section 206 does not name. Under Rule 2-01(c)(2)(iii)(B), what follows for the firm?

options.A: It may not do the audit; that post is an oversight role
options.B: It may continue, as Section 206 names four roles and no others
options.C: It may not do the audit unless the issuer's audit committee approves
options.D: It may continue if the manager stays out of audit-related legal work

questions.key_concept: The SEC's cooling-off rule covers every financial reporting oversight role, such as general counsel, not only the four titles Section 206 names.
questions.pre_read: Compare the titles named in the statute with the roles the SEC's rule covers.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 2-01(c)(2)(iii)(B) applies the cooling-off bar to any financial reporting oversight role, and Rule 2-01(f)(3)(ii) lists general counsel among those roles. The SEC chose this broader test because Section 206 also covers any person in an equivalent position. A former team member who worked on last year's audit now holds such a role, so the firm is not independent. Option B is close but stops at the statute's four titles.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: Section 206 names four titles, but it adds equivalent positions, and the SEC rule covers every financial reporting oversight role, general counsel included.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the audit committee oversees independence. Its approval route under the rule is for emergencies or unusual situations, not an ordinary hire.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because recusal limits influence. But the rule turns on the role the person holds, not on the tasks they avoid.

tips: Eliminate: C offers an audit committee approval the rule keeps for emergencies, and D treats recusal as a cure, though the rule looks at the role held.
Final two: A beats B because Rule 2-01(c)(2)(iii)(B) reaches every financial reporting oversight role, and Rule 2-01(f)(3)(ii) lists general counsel.
Exam cue: for cooling-off hires, test the role against the SEC's financial reporting oversight list, not just the four titles in Section 206.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Conflicts of interest, studies and state regulators. What firm rotation means
questions.question: For its study, Section 207(c) defined the mandatory rotation of registered public accounting firms as:

options.A: replacing the lead audit partner after five consecutive years
options.B: requiring the audit committee to rebid the audit engagement every year
options.C: requiring a new audit firm after any adverse PCAOB inspection
options.D: limiting how long one firm may be an issuer's auditor of record

questions.key_concept: Section 207(c) defines mandatory rotation as a limit on the years a particular firm may be a particular issuer's auditor of record.
questions.pre_read: Recall what the Section 207 study was about, and how it differs from rules already in the Act.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 207(c) defines mandatory rotation as imposing a limit on the period of years in which a particular registered firm may be the auditor of record for a particular issuer. Section 207 ordered only a study of its potential effects and a report to Congress; no section of the Act imposes it. Option A is close, but partner rotation keeps the same firm in place.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: partner rotation changes people within the same firm, which Section 203 already requires; Section 207(c) describes changing the firm itself.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because audit committees may rebid audits. But Section 207(c) defines rotation as a cap on one firm's years as auditor, not an annual tender.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a poor inspection can prompt a change of auditor. But Section 207(c) defines rotation as a fixed cap on a firm's years, not an inspection-triggered switch.

tips: Eliminate: B turns rotation into an annual rebid, and C ties a change of firm to inspection results; Section 207(c) sets a fixed cap on one firm's tenure with one issuer.
Final two: D beats A because Section 207(c) limits a firm's years as auditor of record; replacing a partner leaves the same firm in place.
Exam cue: 'mandatory rotation' in Title II means the firm; partner rotation is a different, binding rule.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Conflicts of interest, studies and state regulators. Pay for selling other services
questions.question: A registered firm with 400 partners pays the lead partner on an issuer's audit a bonus for selling that issuer a cybersecurity review. Under Rule 2-01(c)(8), what is the effect?

options.A: None, if the audit committee preapproved the review in advance
options.B: None, because the review is a permitted non-audit service
options.C: The firm loses its independence from this audit client
options.D: The partner must rotate off, though the firm stays independent

questions.key_concept: An audit partner paid for selling non-audit services to the audit client impairs the firm's independence (Rule 2-01(c)(8)), outside the small-firm exemption.
questions.pre_read: Recall what the SEC rule says about how audit partners may be paid.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 2-01(c)(8) says an accountant is not independent of an audit client if, at any point during the audit and professional engagement period, an audit partner earns or receives compensation based on procuring engagements with that client for services other than audit, review or attest services. A firm this size is outside the small-firm exemption. Option A is close, but preapproval covers the service, not the partner's pay.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: preapproval governs whether the service may be provided, but Rule 2-01(c)(8) targets the partner's pay for selling it, which preapproval does not address.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the review itself may be allowed. But the rule covers pay for selling any non-audit service, permitted or not.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because rotation addresses familiarity. The compensation rule makes the firm lose independence; moving the partner off later does not cure it.

tips: Eliminate: B limits the rule to banned services, though it covers any non-audit sale, and D treats rotation as a cure for an independence breach.
Final two: C beats A because Rule 2-01(c)(8) impairs independence when an audit partner is paid for selling non-audit work to the client; approving the service does not change that.
Exam cue: an audit partner may be rewarded for audit, review and attest work, never for selling the client other services.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Conflicts of interest, studies and state regulators. How the auditor's fee is set
questions.question: Under Rule 2-01(c)(5), an issuer's independent auditor is not independent if, during the audit and professional engagement period, it provides the issuer any service or product:

options.A: costing more in fees than the issuer's annual audit
options.B: for a commission, or for a fee that depends on the result
options.C: for a fee that varies with the complexity of the work
options.D: through an affiliate of the firm located outside the United States

questions.key_concept: Providing any service to an audit client for a contingent fee or a commission impairs the auditor's independence (Rule 2-01(c)(5)).
questions.pre_read: Ask what each fee arrangement is tied to, then compare it with the rule's definitions.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 2-01(c)(5) says an accountant is not independent if, at any point during the audit and professional engagement period, it provides any service or product to an audit client for a contingent fee or a commission, or receives one from the client. Under Rule 2-01(f)(10), a contingent fee depends on a specified finding or result. Option C is close, but the definition says fees may vary with complexity.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because large non-audit fees draw scrutiny. But Rule 2-01 sets no fee-size test; paragraph (c)(5) is about how the fee is set.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a variable fee can look contingent, but Rule 2-01(f)(10) says fees may vary with the complexity of the services without becoming contingent.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because cross-border work raises questions. But the rule's definition of the accounting firm includes its affiliates abroad; location alone does not impair independence.

tips: Eliminate: A invents a fee-size cap that Rule 2-01 does not set, and D treats a foreign affiliate as the problem, though the rule looks at the service and the fee.
Final two: B beats C because Rule 2-01(c)(5) bars fees tied to a finding or result; Rule 2-01(f)(10) lets fees vary with complexity.
Exam cue: on fee questions, ask what the fee depends on: a result or a commission impairs independence; effort and complexity do not.
